title: Tropical Storm Vance forms in eastern Pacific as hurricane season reaches rare milestone not seen since 2018 - FOX Weather
content:
Tropical Storm Vance formed in the Pacific, marking the first V-named storm in the eastern Pacific since 2018. The system has maximum sustained winds of 40 mph and a central pressure of 1,003 mb. The active Pacific continues to churn out tropical systems, with Tropical Storm Vance becoming the latest named storm to develop in the eastern Pacific while Super Typhoon Champi remains a powerful storm in the western Pacific. Tropical Storm Vance has formed in the eastern Pacific south of Mexico, becoming the first V-named storm in the basin since 2018. WHAT’S THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A TROPICAL DEPRESSION, TROPICAL STORM AND HURRICANE? Vance developed from Tropical Depression Twenty-Two-E as conditions remained favorable for tropical development across the region following the dissipation of Tropical Storm Trudy. One factor that may have helped the system organize was a strong Tehuantepecer wind event along southern Mexico. These events occur when cooler, stronger winds are funneled through the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and spill out over the warm waters of the eastern Pacific. SUPER EL NIÑO FUELED WINTER COULD UNLEASH MORE STORMS, DRIVING MORE ACTIVE PATTERN INTO THE SOUTH As those winds push offshore, they can interact with the surrounding tropical environment and increase the amount of spin in the lower atmosphere. When that spin lines up with an existing tropical disturbance and warm ocean waters, it can help thunderstorms organize around a developing area of low pressure. 'EVOLVING CRISIS': COULD EL NIÑO BRING NEEDED RAIN TO THE 2 LARGEST RESERVOIRS IN THE US? Forecast models have suggested Vance could initially move northwest before turning somewhat back toward Mexico. The FOX Forecast Center will continue to monitor for changes in strength and track. NASA SATELLITES REVEAL STRIKING OCEAN COLOR CHANGE AS SUPER EL NIÑO STRENGTHENS Meanwhile, Super Typhoon Champi remains an exceptionally powerful storm in the western Pacific after rapidly intensifying to maximum sustained winds of 185 mph with gusts to 225 mph. At that intensity, Champi tied Super Typhoon Sinlaku as the strongest storm on Earth in 2026. Champi intensified over extremely warm waters with little wind shear and limited dry air nearby, providing an ideal environment for the storm to strengthen. COULD HISTORY REPEAT ITSELF? HOW PAST SUPER EL NIÑO WINTERS OFFER CLUES ABOUT WHAT'S AHEAD The typhoon has also generated enormous seas. Significant wave heights near the storm's center reached 68 feet, representing the average height of the highest one-third of waves. Champi has been tracking west-northwestward and is expected to gradually turn more toward the northwest. Forecast models have differed on its eventual path, with some bringing the storm toward Taiwan and others showing it curving northward toward Japan. The Joint Typhoon Warning Center forecast has favored the recurvature scenario, with Champi eventually approaching Japan this weekend as a weaker typhoon or tropical storm. title: Cadillac's Near-Perfect Escalade-V Officially Gets F1-Inspired Makeover For Mexico - CarBuzz
content: As Formula One grew in popularity during the 21st century, new automakers became interested in joining the sport. Cadillac was among them and announced the formation of a team in 2023. The Cadillac Formula 1 Team began competing during the 2026 season with Sergio Pérez and Valtteri Bottas as its drivers. The inaugural season has been rocky, with the best result so far being Bottas finishing 13th at the 2026 Chinese Grand Prix. While there's not much to celebrate in terms of team performance at the finish line, Cadillac is honoring one of its drivers with a special-edition model. But the company is only making a handful of them, all of which will be sold south of the border. Sergio Pérez is better known by his nickname Checo, and Cadillac is using that moniker for its Escalade-V Checo Pérez Edition. The driver is from Mexico and races using the number 11, so Caddy is limiting this version to just 11 units, exclusively for Mexico. The Cadillac Escalade-V Checo Pérez Edition comes with a variety of special styling touches. The Escalade and V-Series emblems are black, and the Cadillac badge has a monochromatic color scheme. There's also illumination for the grille and door handles. The engine cover features an exposed carbon-fiber finish. The puddle lights project a V-Series graphic on the ground, and the interior features a set of sport pedals. The SUV rides on 24-inch wheels with a Satin Graphite finish. Buyers also get a welcome kit to accompany the special edition. Each special-edition Escalade-V also comes with two plaques identifying the vehicle's production number out of the 11 examples and Pérez's signature. One of them is on the exterior B-pillar, and the other is on the interior center console. Beyond these styling tweaks, the Cadillac Escalade-V Checo Pérez Edition is like any other version of this performance SUV. Power comes from a supercharged 6.2-liter V8 that makes 682 horsepower and 653 pound-feet of torque. A 10-speed automatic transmission sends the output to an all-wheel-drive system with an electronic limited-slip differential. It rides on General Motors’ Magnetic Ride Control adaptive suspension and features six-piston Brembo front brakes. Even the performance-oriented V model is still an Escalade, so it needs luxury to complement the speed. The special-edition models come standard with the 55-inch curved pillar-to-pillar screen with a multicolor head-up display. The occupants can enjoy music from a 36-speaker AKG Studio Reference stereo. The advanced driving assistance systems include a 360-degree camera system, parking assist, front pedestrian and cyclist detection, rear pedestrian detection, cross-traffic alert, and braking assistance. The second row also comes with executive seats that feature heating, ventilation, six-way adjustment, lumbar massage, and folding trays. These occupants also get a pair of 12.6-inch screens. Some unique badges and trim pieces barely seem like enough to justify an 11-unit special edition. However, there are some hardcore F1 fans out there, and such a small production run means that Cadillac isn't taking too big of a gamble with the Checo Pérez Edition. The 11 examples of the Cadillac Escalade-V Checo Pérez Edition are available to order in Mexico as of October 20, 2026. They cost 4,099,000 Mexican pesos ($220,510 at current exchange rates). For comparison, the regular model begins at 3,847,500 Mexican pesos ($206,980). In the US, the Escalade-V begins at $124,700 (before a $2,895 destination fee). title: Gibson Celebrates Tom Petty’s 50th Anniversary With Five Limited-Edition Flying V Guitars - That Eric Alper
content: Tom Petty spent much of his career making rock ‘n’ roll sound wonderfully uncomplicated, even when the work behind it was anything but. Now Gibson is celebrating 50 years of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers with something appropriately loud, unmistakably stylish and remarkably limited: five Flying V guitars inspired by the band’s original logo, with just 50 instruments available in each finish worldwide. The collection, affectionately named the “Flying Five”, takes its inspiration from the Heartbreakers logo featured on the band’s self-titled 1976 debut album. With only 250 guitars being produced in total, Gibson has turned one of rock’s most recognizable silhouettes into a tribute to one of America’s most enduring bands. And the guitars come in five striking finishes: Gainesville Gold, Graphite Metallic, Heartbreaker Red, Pearl White Metallic and Pelham Blue. It’s a fitting combination of rock history and guitar mythology. The Flying V has always looked like an instrument designed for somebody who intended to make an entrance, and Petty understood the power of a memorable image as well as anybody. His daughter, Adria Petty, sees the connection as especially meaningful. “The Heartbreakers logo has been part of the band’s identity since the first album, so seeing Gibson reinterpret it through the Flying V 50th anniversary edition feels overdue, as they have been part of the story since the beginning,” she explains. She also recalls that the V was an essential part of her father’s stage imagery during the band’s rise to fame in the 1970s. The guitar’s relationship to that history runs deeper than its outline. Each anniversary Flying V features a mahogany body and neck, a SlimTaper neck profile and a rosewood fretboard with 22 medium jumbo frets. Gibson has equipped the instruments with a pair of ’70s Tribute humbucker pickups, hand-wired electronics, individual volume controls and a master tone control featuring an Orange Drop capacitor. Gold-plated hardware, Grover Rotomatic tuners and a three-ply white pickguard complete the design, alongside a special Heartbreaker 50th truss rod cover and a reproduction of Petty’s signature on the back of the headstock. For players, the specifications provide a fully functional rock instrument. For collectors, the limited production and unmistakable visual references offer a direct connection to the Heartbreakers’ history. A great commemorative guitar should inspire somebody to take it out of its case and play. Petty’s legacy is far too closely connected to the joy of making music for an instrument bearing his name to spend its entire life hanging silently on a wall. Gibson has extended that thinking into a broader anniversary collection, developed in collaboration with the Tom Petty Estate. The accompanying lifestyle range draws from the band’s visual history, vintage touring merchandise and Petty’s distinctive personal style. Rather than creating designs entirely from scratch, Gibson sent a team to the Tom Petty Clubhouse in Van Nuys, California, where they examined artifacts from across the Heartbreakers’ career. That research became the foundation for a collection of clothing, accessories and memorabilia designed to capture the lived-in character of the band’s history. At the estate’s request, Gibson partnered with Nashville heritage clothing brand Imogene+Willie to develop several pieces, including four American-made graphic T-shirts featuring Tom Petty, Dogs with Wings, DIY Band and Heartbreaker designs. The shirts are made from American cotton, then garment-washed and preshrunk to recreate the comfortable feel of a favourite piece of vintage concert merchandise. Alongside a green military-style patch jacket and a black backstage work jacket, the collection includes a limited-edition leather jacket created through a collaboration between Imogene+Willie, Gibson and Schott N.Y.C. The design takes its inspiration from the jacket Petty wore on the cover of the Heartbreakers’ 1976 debut album. Its striped satin lining also references the black-and-white blazer he wore on the cover of the UK single for “Listen to Her Heart” in 1978. Only 75 of the leather jackets will be produced worldwide. It’s an unusually detailed tribute to a musician whose personal style became closely connected with the sound and identity of his band. Petty had a gift for making rock-star clothing look like something he’d owned for years. The jackets, shirts and accessories in the new collection attempt to preserve that effortless visual personality. There are smaller collectibles, too, including a “Last All Night” Zippo lighter, a bandana, a miniature Flying V guitar from Axe Heaven, a Tom Petty cap, a guitar strap, a pick tin and a sticker set. The collection arrives during an especially significant anniversary year for Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers. On November 6, the Tom Petty Estate will release ‘Origins 1971–1978’, a box set exploring Petty’s early recording career, the formation of the Heartbreakers and the band’s first years together. The set combines rare, live and previously unreleased recordings with the group’s first two albums, offering a substantial look at the period when Petty and his bandmates were developing the sound that would eventually make them rock legends. That early history provides the perfect context for Gibson’s new guitars. The Heartbreakers’ debut introduced the world to a band whose approach to songwriting balanced the directness of rock ‘n’ roll with an extraordinary melodic instinct. Petty’s music could sound deceptively simple, yet those songs were built with the kind of precision that allowed them to remain familiar and beloved across generations. By the time Petty and the Heartbreakers were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2002, their catalogue had become a defining part of American rock history. But the music’s enduring popularity has always depended on something beyond awards and recognition. Petty wrote songs that people could carry into their own lives. His melodies became companions on long drives, his lyrics captured stubborn independence and his band understood how to deliver rock ‘n’ roll with confidence and personality. There’s something satisfying about celebrating that history with an instrument that invites another musician to make noise. Gibson Chief Marketing Officer Beth Heidt describes the project as an opportunity to connect longtime fans with younger players discovering Petty’s music. The guitars and clothing are available now through Gibson Garage locations and online, with the extremely limited production making the instruments particularly collectible. Fifty years after the Heartbreakers’ debut, the band’s visual identity remains instantly recognizable, and the songs continue to find new listeners. A Flying V inspired by the group’s earliest artwork brings that history into the hands of musicians who might be discovering Tom Petty for the first time. Rock ‘n’ roll has always been particularly good at passing things between generations. Sometimes it’s a song. Sometimes it’s a guitar. And occasionally, it’s a gold-plated Flying V that looks like it belongs in the middle of a very loud chorus. Eric Alper is a 6-time nominee for Publicist of the Year during Canadian Music Week and has overseen the publicity campaigns for over 183 JUNO Award-nominated albums (and 16 in 2025), 45 Grammy-nominated albums, including 47 JUNO Award, 58 Canadian Folk Music Award, 126 Maple Blues Award-winning albums and is also truly honoured to work with some of the biggest and most important artists of our time.

title: Mānoa: Legendary UH submersible Pisces V begins new chapter at Bishop Museum - University of Hawaii System
content:
After nearly four decades of uncovering historic mysteries of the Pacific Ocean, the deep-sea submersible Pisces V is embarking on a new journey on land. The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa donated the legendary three-person research vessel to the Bernice Pauahi Bishop Museum, ensuring that its legacy of deep-ocean exploration, volcanic research and historic maritime discoveries will be preserved for generations to come. “The donation ensures the submersible’s storied past will be celebrated and shared with museum visitors from Hawai‘i and around the world,” said Chip Fletcher, dean of the UH Mānoa School of Ocean and Earth Science and Technology, home of the Hawaiʻi Undersea Research Laboratory (HURL). HURL operated Pisces V along with its sister submersible, Pisces IV, for decades. However, after years in storage with no prospect of federal funding for refurbishment or redeployment, UH made the decision to entrust the historic craft to the museum. In 1985, UH acquired Pisces V, anchoring HURL’s growing undersea capabilities. Its unique maneuverability, size and depth range, operating at depths up to 6,500 feet, made it the ideal platform for navigating complex terrain and gracefully exploring delicate ecosystems. “Operating as the only U.S. deep submergence facility based in the Pacific Rim, HURL’s work with Pisces V revolutionized oceanography across several fronts,” said Terry Kerby, veteran Pisces V pilot and HURL operations director. “The submersibles were fine-tuned to adapt to the demands of operating effectively in the wide range of terrain and conditions of undersea volcanoes, seamounts in Papahānaumokuākea and beyond, maritime heritage site surveys, salvage operations of lost instruments and vehicles, and decades of pipeline support for the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawai‘i Authority cold water pipe systems. It is exciting to see the Pisces V and this legacy preserved at the Bishop Museum.” Close to home, Pisces V, enabled unprecedented exploration of the seamounts and coral reefs of the Main and Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. The submersible made more dives on Hawaiʻi’s active underwater volcano, Kamaʻehuakanaloa (previously known as Lōʻihi Seamount), than any other submersible. HURL submersibles also pioneered research on mesophotic and deep-sea coral reefs off Maui and throughout the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, conducting vital impact assessments on commercial fishing damage. Throughout the Pacific basin, the submersible ferried teams of researchers on voyages of discovery to places no human had seen before. In 2005, Pisces V embarked on a five-month expedition across the Pacific, exploring active submarine volcanoes along the Kermadec Arc near New Zealand. “Each of these dives were unique, each different,” Kerby shared. “We discovered multiple new species and by combining submersible operations with human divers, we explored deep-sea coral ecosystems in a new way.” Under Kerby’s piloting, Pisces V unlocked famous historical mysteries on the ocean floor. Highlights include locating the Japanese midget submarine sunk by the USS Ward hours before the December 7, 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, as well as locating massive World War II Japanese aircraft-carrying submarines I-400, I-401, and I-14 off Oʻahu.Preserving a legacy at Bishop Museum Though HURL’s operations changed dramatically in 2012 when funding ended, the research and technical teams preserved the Pisces V and its priceless 35-year video and biological data archive. Now, the donation to the Bishop Museum opens a vibrant new chapter. “The Museum has a long and productive history of partnership with the University of Hawai‘i and the Hawai‘i Undersea Research Laboratory,” said Richard Pyle, Senior Curator of Ichthyology and Director of Natural Sciences at Bishop Museum. “Researchers at the Museum have done many dives within these subs over the decades, and our collections hold more than 1,000 scientifically important specimens the sub has collected over the years. It’s very exciting that we can help perpetuate the incredible legacy of these submersibles, and honor the people who fortified that legacy.” In addition to sharing the history of exploration and celebrating the dedicated engineers, pilots, and support crews whose ingenuity made thousands of safe dives possible, the Pisces V’s presence at the museum will inspire future generations of explorers and spark curiosity in ocean science, volcanology, and marine heritage among visitors. “Above all, we want to make sure the important legacy of these submarines is maintained and communicated to our visitors at the Museum,” said Kris Helgen, president and CEO of Bishop Museum. “The role of Bishop Museum involves telling the stories that matter to Hawai‘i and the Pacific, including stories of ocean exploration. We are thrilled to have the Pisces V on our campus.” Though her sea days have concluded, Pisces V will continue her mission on shore—teaching visitors about the vast, dark world beneath the waves that she spent a lifetime illuminating. title: Cadillac’s Rarest Escalade V Yet Honors F1 Driver Checo Perez, And You Can’t Buy One - HotCars
content: Cadillac just built one of the smallest production runs the brand has put out in years, and American buyers can't touch it. The Escalade V Checo Perez Edition caps production at exactly 11 units, matching the racing number Sergio Perez has carried through his Formula 1 career, and every single one is allocated to Mexico. Cadillac revealed the truck on October 19 at the U.S. Ambassador's Residence in Mexico City, with Perez himself on hand, days before the F1 calendar heads to Austin and then to the Mexico City Grand Prix. It's part of a broader push tied to Cadillac's F1 team and its new cowboy-inspired livery, but the Escalade V is the piece enthusiasts will actually want to track down, even knowing they can't. Don't expect a tune. The supercharged 6.2-liter V8 carries over unchanged, still making 682 horsepower and 653 lb-ft of torque, still good for a 4.4-second sprint to 60 mph in a three-row SUV that weighs north of 6,000 pounds. Cadillac didn't touch the Brembo six-piston front brakes, the Magnetic Ride Control dampers, the electronic limited-slip diff, or the 10-speed automatic either. This edition is about standing out in a parking lot, not a drag strip. That means blacked-out badging in a finish distinct from the standard Escalade V's black package, monochromatic Cadillac logos front and rear, an exposed carbon fiber engine cover, aluminum pedals, and ground-projection lighting that throws down V-Series graphics when you unlock the doors. Each truck carries two numbered plaques, 1/11 through 11/11, signed by Perez and mounted on the B-pillar and center console. Buyers also get an exclusive welcome kit, and the whole thing is offered only in black or white, the two colors tied directly to Cadillac's F1 livery. Cadillac moves tens of thousands of Escalades a year. Eleven units against that volume makes this one of the tightest factory special-edition runs any American brand has attempted in recent memory, closer in spirit to a homologation special than a trim package. Perez was Cadillac's first signed driver before Valtteri Bottas joined, and GM Mexico framed the edition as a tribute to both his career and the V-Series brand's 20-plus years of existence, with Perez involved in the design process from the start. Pricing lands at 4,099,000 Mexican pesos, roughly $222,500 at current exchange rates, a premium of about $251,500 pesos over a standard Escalade V. Sales opened through Cadillac dealers in Mexico on October 20. That's the part that stings for American enthusiasts. There's no waitlist workaround, no dealer allocation trick, no special order path north of the border. All 11 are staying in Mexico. Perez himself has 300 Grands Prix coming up at the Mexico City race on November 1, and this truck is built to mark that run, not to court a U.S. audience. It's a reminder that scarcity plays don't always flow the direction enthusiasts expect. Cadillac could have built this for the U.S. market and sold out in a day. Instead, it's a Mexico-only tribute, and the rest of us just get to look. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. title: The Supreme Court Upholds Preliminary Injunction in Kingdom v. Trump,… - Human Rights Campaign
content:
by

                Aneesha Pappy
              
•
                October 21, 2026 HRC President Kelley Robinson: “This decision protects trans inmates from the administration’s attempt to steamroll constitutional rights for now, but the fight to uphold the dignity and respect our community deserves is far from over.” WASHINGTON, DC— Today, the Supreme Court upheld the lower court’s preliminary injunction in Kingdom v. Trump, blocking Trump’s executive order that prohibits the federal Bureau of Prisons from providing transition-related medical care to transgender incarcerated people in federal facilities while the case moves through the courts. Human Rights Campaign President Kelley Robinson released the following statement: “Today, trans people in federal prisons can keep getting the care they need. Denying access to critical medical care for incarcerated people simply because they are trans is discriminatory, cruel and flies in the face of our Eighth Amendment protections. Trump and MAGA extremists are obsessed with targeting our community and undermining access to essential healthcare, defying the recommendations of every major medical association in the country. This decision protects incarcerated trans people from the administration’s attempt to steamroll over constitutional rights for now, but the fight to uphold the dignity and respect our community deserves is far from over.” Kingdom v. Trump challenges an executive order issued earlier this year by Trump prohibiting the federal Bureau of Prisons from providing transition-related medical care for incarcerated transgender people in federal prisons and detention centers. The executive order also mandated the transfer of transgender women held in federal facilities to men’s facilities. With support by the ACLU, the ACLU of DC and the Transgender Law Center, the class action lawsuit was filed on behalf of three transgender inmates, arguing that the executive order violates the U.S. Constitution’s Eighth Amendment protections against “cruel and unusual punishments” by denying access to medically-necessary healthcare. In June of this year, the plaintiffs were granted a preliminary injunction blocking the enforcement of the executive order by a federal district court judge — which has now been upheld. The case will continue to be adjudicated in the District Court for the District of Columbia. The Human Rights Campaign (HRC) is the nation’s largest LGBTQ+ civil rights organization working to achieve equality for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer (LGBTQ+) people, with 4 million members and supporters. From the courtroom to the classroom, from Congress to corporate America, HRC and the HRC Foundation build power through partnerships, storytelling, and action—working to create a future rooted in equity, freedom and belonging for all LGBTQ+ people. title: The Beginning of the End - The Bulwark
content: I took Flash to the ballpark for the first time when he was about 16 months old. We had a minor league team down the road from our house. One Saturday afternoon, he woke up from his nap and we caught two innings in the middle of a day game. We left as soon as he got bored. For several years, that was his experience of baseball. We would show up in the middle of the game and stay for ten minutes, or an hour, and leave when he was ready. We made it to the end of a game for the first time when he was 5 and the conclusion of the ninth inning confused him. “Baseball is over?” he asked. In that moment I realized that, from his perspective, baseball was like the sea. It was always there. He showed up at the ballpark and baseball was happening; he left the ballpark and baseball was happening. In his imagination, baseball never stopped. The players were always there, playing, and we just visited baseball. It never occurred to him that baseball was a finite thing with a beginning, a middle, and an end. The Bulwark is reader-supported—which makes all our independent journalism possible. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Two Saturdays ago, Flash pitched in college for the first time. It was just fall ball; a friendly. Nothing important. The coach gave him an inning of work. He did a nice job. My heart was happy and proud. But also confused. And a little sad. Because I realized that unless he gets drafted after college, this was the last “first time” of his baseball journey. And the last first time of my baseball journey with him. I remember all of the first times. That first game with his chubby cheeks. The first catch in our front yard. The first time I took him to a field where he could run the bases. As he got older, we were at the minor league park all the time. I remember the first time he caught a foul ball and the first time he worked up the nerve to talk to one of the players. Over the years he became friendly with a bunch of them. Baseball was the only thing he wanted to do. And because he saw these guys up close, and knew them, he assumed that it was normal. That becoming a ballplayer was something anyone could just decide to do; like going to law school. I kept him out of the maw of organized baseball for as long as possible. I didn’t want to get sucked into the Kids’ Sports Industrial Complex. When he was 10, I finally relented and let him join Little League. The firsts kept piling up. First travel-team game. First home run. First complete game. First immaculate inning. First middle school game. First no hitter. First high school varsity game. First showcase. For seventeen years, baseball was a thing Flash and I did together. It was always there. Like the sea. As I watched him throw his first college pitch I realized that this constant in our lives isn’t actually constant. It has a beginning, a middle, and an end. Some day baseball with Flash will be over. I know that’s too narrow a view. In the most important ways, baseball really is like the sea. It really is always there. What changes is our relationship to it. Because there have also been a bunch of other baseball firsts for me and Flash. Our first major league game. Our first World Series game. Our first post-COVID game. Our first trip to Cooperstown. Our first night at Fenway. Someday, God willing, there will be new kinds of firsts. For the two of us, then for him with his own kids, me with my grandkids. And then for him and his grandkids. I’ll pass away, but that stuff about the rhythm of baseball binding together the generations? It’s true. All of it. Here’s a funny thing: I’ve never played a single game of baseball. Not once. Never even threw, or caught, a baseball until I was in college. I have no personal connection to the game. For me, it’s inextricably linked with Flash. For me, the joy of baseball has been walking with my little boy as he grew. Someday his part in playing the game of baseball will end. But I’ll still get to walk with him. Once I realized that, I understood that sadness has no place here. Only gratitude. Thanks for letting me share this with you. It means a lot to me. This piece is a reminder that there is a season for true grief. And that the only way through is together: On the last Sunday afternoon of September, Rhenda Strub was bundled up against the autumn chill for one final day at the ballpark, eating Cracker Jack and sweet and spicy pickles. . . . After she lost her 27-year-old son, Wyatt, to muscular dystrophy three years ago, she retreated to his room and spent countless hours alone quilting and watching baseball games on television. The constancy of baseball helped to structure her days, but the loneliness only added to her grief. So at the beginning of this season, Ms. Strub bought two season tickets to the Mariners in Section 120, on the first base side, thinking she would regularly go with her loved ones to T-Mobile Park. But her husband doesn’t like crowds, and the rest of her family has busy lives. So she wrote a post on Facebook — with some trepidation, she said, because the “internet can be a cruel place” — asking strangers if they wanted to attend games with her. . . . By the end of this baseball season, Ms. Strub had attended games with about 30 strangers and found that the people she connected with needed her as much as she needed them. She built an online community, bringing together the people she had met in a private Facebook group, calling the project “Strangers to Friends.” If she couldn’t attend a game — she had to miss a few when her husband, Mike, had brain surgery — she handed off her tickets to strangers who had reached out to her but didn’t know each other. She said she was “gobsmacked” by the reaction to her post. “I have made so many friends this summer,” she said. “I have friends that will be my friends for the rest of my life.” I needed to read this piece, this week. I hope you’ll read it, too. It made me think of you guys in our Bulwark world and how we help each other. The Bulwark is reader-supported—which makes all our independent journalism possible. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Well, at least it’s nice to be in tears about something sweet and sentimental instead of something related to our daily fresh hell. Even with all of your incredible accomplishments, JVL, clearly fatherhood outranks most others, if not all. That was a beautiful piece JVL. title: Beau Brungard Named NFF William V. Campbell Trophy Finalist - Youngstown State Athletics
content:
Beau Brungard Named NFF William V. Campbell Trophy Finalist YSU QB Beau Brungard has been named one of the finalists for the 2026 National Football Foundation William V. Campbell Trophy®, the National Football Foundation (NFF) & College Hall of Fame announced today. The William V. Campbell Trophy® is college football's premier scholar-athlete award that annually recognizes an individual as the absolute best in the nation for his combined academic success, football performance and exemplary leadership. This prestigious award is given to only 18 finalists across all levels of NCAA divisions including NAIA. Each finalist will receive an $18,000 postgraduate scholarship as a member of the 2026 NFF National Scholar-Athlete Class Presented by Fidelity Investments®. Brungard is one of only two players representing the FCS this year, joining him is Montana State offensive lineman, Titan Fleischmann. A dynamic dual-threat quarterback and the 2025 Walter Payton Award winner as the top player in the FCS, Beau Brungard has rewritten the Youngstown State record books while excelling in the classroom. The New Middletown, Ohio, native becomes the Penguins' second NFF National Scholar-Athlete and first since 1998. Having graduated summa cum laude in May with a degree in business administration, Brungard is currently pursuing an MBA. A two-time CSC Academic All-District selection and two-time First Team Academic All-Missouri Valley Football Conference (MVFC) honoree, he has also earned recognition on the Dean's List. A unanimous First Team All-American in 2025, Brungard also claimed the Walter Camp Foundation FCS Player of the Year Award, FCS ADA Offensive Player of the Year honors and MVFC Offensive Player of the Year accolades. A two-time First Team All-MVFC selection, he led the FCS last season in total offense (4,702 yards) and points responsible for (326), becoming the first player in FCS history to pass for more than 300 yards and rush for 200 yards in a single game. He also set the MVFC single-game rushing record for a quarterback with 264 yards against Robert Morris. Brungard continues to rewrite the YSU record books, holding career marks for total offense (10,786 yards), offensive plays (1,524) and rushing touchdowns (57) and counting. Through eight games in 2026, he has passed for 2,061 yards and 19 touchdowns while rushing for 647 yards and 11 scores. Against Indiana State on Oct. 10, he threw for a career-high 386 yards and three touchdowns while rushing for two more scores, breaking Youngstown State's all-time career rushing touchdowns record. This season, he ranks first nationally in points responsible for per game (23.0), second in total offense (338.5 yards per game), sixth in passing yards (2,061) and sixth in total points scored (68). He leads the MVFC in multiple categories, including total offense, passing yards, pass completions and rushing touchdowns. A two-year team captain, Brungard led the Penguins to the 2025 FCS Playoffs and a final No. 19 national ranking. His leadership has helped YSU earn a 6-2 record and a No. 4 AFCA national ranking. His father, Mark, quarterbacked the Penguins from 1992-95, helping YSU capture national championships in 1993 and 1994. Off the field, Brungard leads team Bible study sessions and organizes a summer youth football camp. He also mentors local children individually and represents Youngstown State at numerous community and university functions. "The Campbell Trophy represents everything right in college football," said NFF Chairman Archie Manning, whose sons Peyton (a Campbell Trophy® recipient) and Eli were NFF National Scholar-Athletes in 1997 and 2003, respectively. "These 18 finalists have competed at an extraordinary level while embracing the demands of the classroom and making a meaningful difference in their communities. They understand that success is about more than what happens on Saturdays, and we are proud to recognize them as examples of the character, discipline and leadership that make college football so special." The finalists will travel to the Bellagio Resort & Casino in Las Vegas for the 68th NFF Annual Awards Dinner Presented by Las Vegas on Dec. 8, where their accomplishments will be highlighted in front of one of the most powerful audiences in all of sports. Live during the event, one member of the class will be declared as the winner of the 37th Campbell Trophy® and have his postgraduate scholarship increased to $25,000. title: Three Como players who can make an impact v Manchester United - Yahoo Sports
content: Serie A side Como play a historic Champions League tie against Manchester United today. While there have been fears that the tie could be postponed, it is set to go ahead, with the Red Devils set to face a huge challenge as well. Cesc Fabregas' side play a fluid brand of football, where they constantly exchange positions rapidly, which allows them to build from the back smoothly and transition from midfield to attack swiftly. More than the system, it is specific players that will be key for Como. Apart from the obvious names, here are three players who could be huge today. At just 21, Jacobo Ramon has become one of the best centre-backs in Serie A. He impresses with his ability on the ball, having fulfilled the promise that was seen during his early days at Real Madrid. The talent is a perfect fit for the setup, which brings the most out of him, also allowing him to sometimes step into midfield. While not a Spain international yet, Ramon's time could indeed soon come. The ex-Manchester City player is one of the most silent impact players in the Como side. He uses his left foot to dictate the tempo of games at will, breaking it up when needed too. He plays a big role in allowing Como to build up efficiently, dropping into the backline when needed and also sometimes drifting wide for the same purpose. He generally doesn't get enough plaudits either but a big game against Manchester United could the right time for him to get the credit he deserves. A much more prominent name due to his heroics in the last few months, Martin Baturina has been more important for Como than Nico Paz since 2026 started. His importance grew after a slow start and he is constantly among the goals. The Croatian floats around in attack, picking up the ball in the right spaces as he roams from one flank to the other and has a hammer of a right foot. When Baturina gets the ball, it feels like everything slows down before the takes an action. He has deceptive 1v1 ability too, which can be a big threat for Manchester United.

title: Crystal Palace 'handball' goal v Forest not a VAR error - panel - Yahoo Sports
content: The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel says Crystal Palace's second goal against Nottingham Forest should have been disallowed on the field for handball - but backed the video assistant referee's decision not to intervene. The game was locked at 1-1 deep into first-half stoppage time when Jefferson Lerma appeared to nod the ball through the legs of Forest keeper Matz Sels. However, it soon transpired that the ball had deflected off the elbow of team-mate Anan Khalail on its way into goal. That meant the goal technically belonged to Khalail, who could not score a goal with his arm. This was not picked up in the initial replays, only becoming clear during the half-time analysis on the television coverage. Palace went on to win the game 3-1 at Selhurst Park. The Premier League's KMI Panel voted 3:2 that it was an on-field mistake by referee Peter Bankes, but it was unanimous that the VAR, Darren England, was right not to rule out the goal. "On the balance of probability the ball is likely to have come into contact with Khalaili's arm," the KMI Panel said. "The panel all supported the VAR's decision to not intervene on the basis that the footage readily available to the VAR doesn't show conclusive evidence of a handball." It will sting for Forest as they had a Neco Williams goal ruled out for handball in their 0-0 draw with Tottenham through a VAR intervention. Williams insisted after the game the ball did not touch his arm, but replays which later emerged appeared to prove it did. The KMI Panel unanimously supported the decision. Bankes was on VAR duty for the disallowed goal against Spurs.

title: Harding's Andrew Miller Named Finalist for Prestigious 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy® - Harding University Athletics
content: SEARCY, Ark. — Harding University senior All-America running back Andrew Miller has been selected as a finalist for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy®, college football's premier scholar-athlete award, the National Football Foundation & College Hall of Fame (NFF) announced Wednesday morning. Recognized universally as the "Academic Heisman," the Campbell Trophy® celebrates its 37th year honoring the nation's absolute best football scholar-athlete for combined academic success, football performance, and exemplary community leadership. As a finalist, Miller is officially named a member of the prestigious 2026 NFF National Scholar-Athlete Class Presented by Fidelity Investments and will receive an $18,000 postgraduate scholarship. Miller's selection marks the second consecutive season a Harding student-athlete has received the honor. He becomes only the second player in program history to achieve the distinction, following in the footsteps of his cousin, former All-American defensive back Ty Dugger, who was named a Campbell Trophy® finalist and NFF National Scholar-Athlete in 2025. Miller and the elite class of finalists will travel to Las Vegas to be honored at the 68th NFF Annual Awards Dinner Presented by Las Vegas on Tuesday, Dec. 8, at the Bellagio Resort & Casino. During the black-tie ceremony before college football's most distinguished gathering, one member of the class will be declared the outright winner of the 37th Campbell Trophy® and have his postgraduate scholarship elevated to $25,000. Miller was selected from a record pool of 206 semifinalists across all divisions of college football (FBS, FCS, Division II, Division III, and NAIA) and stands as one of only a select few non-FBS student-athletes in the nation chosen for this ultimate collegiate honor. "Andrew represents everything that is right about college athletics and Harding University," said Harding head coach Roddy Mote. "To compete at a national championship level week in and week out while maintaining relentless dedication to his academics and serving others in the community requires an extraordinary level of discipline and character. Our entire football family, university, and community could not be prouder of Andrew on this well-deserved national honor." A native of Searcy, Arkansas, Miller maintains a 3.66 cumulative grade-point average as a kinesiology major and is on pace to graduate in December 2026 under the leadership of Harding Athletics Director Jeff Morgan and Faculty Athletics Representative Stephen Burks. A 2025 College Sports Communicators (CSC) First-Team Academic All-American and Academic All-District selection, Miller is a four-time Dean's List honoree and a two-time Great American Conference Academic Honor Roll recipient. On the field, Miller has etched his name among the most decorated running backs in collegiate history while anchoring the backfield for the consensus second-ranked Bisons (7-0). A 2026 team captain and three-year letterman, Miller was a consensus First-Team All-American and First-Team All-GAC selection in 2025 while finishing as the national runner-up for the Harlon Hill Trophy, presented to the top player in NCAA Division II. He also claimed the 2025 Darren McFadden Award as the top collegiate running back in the state of Arkansas. During the 2025 campaign, Miller shattered six Harding single-season records, including rushing yards (2,048) and rushing touchdowns (28)—both of which ranked second nationally in Division II. He also set HU's single-game rushing record with 298 yards and four touchdowns on 21 carries against Henderson State. Entering this fall with 3,618 career rushing yards (4th in HU history) and 50 rushing touchdowns (3rd in HU history), Miller enters Week 8 as the active career leader across all divisions of NCAA football (FBS, FCS, D-II, and D-III) in both rushing yards (4,526) and rushing touchdowns (65). His 65 career scores leave him just one shy of Cole Chancey's all-time Harding program record (66). Through seven games in 2026, Miller has carried 152 times for 908 yards and 15 touchdowns, leading the Great American Conference in both rushing yards and rushing touchdowns. Nationally, Miller ranks third in Division II in rushing touchdowns (15), fifth in total points scored (90), fifth in scoring (12.9 ppg), and seventh in both rushing yards (908) and rushing yards per game (129.7 ypg) for an offense that paces NCAA Division II with 417.1 rushing yards per game. Miller played an instrumental role in guiding Harding to a perfect 15-0 record and the 2023 NCAA Division II National Championship, followed by an appearance in the 2025 national championship game as national runners-up. He also led the Bisons to the Super Region 3 final and a No. 4 national ranking in 2024, securing three consecutive Great American Conference championships and a remarkable 42-3 team record during his first three collegiate seasons. Beyond the field and classroom, Miller has demonstrated an exceptional commitment to community leadership. Throughout his collegiate career, he has been an active participant in Harding's Bison Buddies program, visiting local Searcy elementary schools on a weekly basis to mentor young students. Additionally, Miller regularly volunteers his time at area youth football camps. "We are extremely proud to announce the finalists for the 2026 Campbell Trophy®," said NFF Chairman Archie Manning. "These young men have achieved extraordinary success on the field, in the classroom, and within their communities. They represent the absolute best of college football, embodying leadership, discipline, and high moral character. We look forward to honoring Andrew and his fellow classmates in Las Vegas this December." "The NFF National Scholar-Athlete Awards are the cornerstone of the National Football Foundation's mission," said NFF President & CEO Steve Hatchell. "The Campbell Trophy® finalists showcase the power of football to cultivate elite leaders who excel across every facet of life. Andrew Miller exemplifies that standard at the highest level." Miller and the No. 2-ranked Bisons return to action this Saturday, Oct. 24, traveling to Monticello, Arkansas, to face Great American Conference foe Arkansas-Monticello at Willis "Convoy" Leslie Cotton Bowl Stadium. The guitar is limited to a total run of 250 in five colors Gibson is celebrating the 50th anniversary of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers with a limited run of Flying V guitars, as well as a new apparel collection. The Flying V is inspired by Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers’ self-titled 1976 debut album, which features a Flying V guitar piercing a heart on its cover. The guitar comes in five colors — Gainesville Gold, Graphite Metallic, Heartbreaker Red, Pearl White Metallic, and Pelham Blue — limited to 50 each, for a total run of just 250. The late Tom Petty’s daughter Adria stated, “The Heartbreakers logo has been part of the band’s identity since the first album, so seeing Gibson reinterpret it through the Flying V 50th anniversary edition feels overdue as they have been part of the story since the beginning. The V was an essential part of the imagery onstage for my dad as well as the band rose to fame in the 1970’s. The collection honors Tom and the Heartbreakers’ history while giving musicians and fans a new way to carry that spirit forward.” In addition to the limited-edition guitars, Gibson has unveiled a Tom Petty apparel collection, featuing T-shirts, a leather jacket, hats, belts, and more. The guitars and the apparel are available at Gibson.com, although most of the guitar styles are sold out already. title: Hull City v Brentford - Match preview, kick-off time & more - Brentford FC
content:
Analysis, team news, match officials and more. Here's everything you need to know ahead of Brentford's Premier League game against Hull City at MKM Stadium on Sunday (2pm kick-off GMT, live on Sky Sports) Analysis, team news, match officials and more - here's everything you need to know ahead of the game. Brentford travel to Humberside to take on Sergej Jakirović's Hull City this Sunday, with the Tigers looking to bounce back after a narrow loss at Fulham. Promoted via the Championship play-offs last season, Hull have made a flying start after a nine-year absence from the top flight, recording back-to-back wins over Manchester United and Coventry. The Tigers followed up those victories with creditable draws against Aston Villa, Chelsea and Everton, and they currently sit ninth in the Premier League, a point behind sixth-placed Brentford. Incisive, direct football and defensive resilience have underpinned the Tigers' strong showing on their return to the top tier, but their Bosnian head coach was scathing in his assessment of last weekend's 1-0 defeat at Fulham. "We were very, very poor," admitted Jakirović. "We collapsed together; it's also my responsibility." Dominated for much of that contest in west London, Jakirović has hinted at a shake-up of his starting XI, but will he tweak his tactics? Thus far, the Tigers have allowed their opponents the lion's share of possession, defended deep and launched lightning raids forward, their threat from open play complemented by considerable set-piece strength. Hull have averaged just 32 per cent possession this season, with their open-play sequences containing an average of only 2.53 passes. Brentford will therefore have opportunities to bring the ball down, but finding a way through the Tigers' well-organised defence could prove challenging. Brentford are likely to need patience, precision and variation in their attacking play and, despite Vitaly Janelt and Yehor Yarmoliuk’s suspensions, their available midfielders appear well-suited to the challenge. Mathias Jensen and Mikkel Damsgaard number among the most intelligent passers in the Premier League, and their ability to unlock deep-lying defences could come in very handy on Sunday. Mamadou Sangaré, meanwhile, impressed after his introduction as a second-half sub against Liverpool, and his energy and tenacity could provide the perfect foil for Brentford's Danish duo. Hull have been particularly resilient at MKM Stadium, however, conceding just twice on home soil this season, a record bettered only by Brighton (one conceded). Remarkably, the Tigers have achieved this despite averaging just 29 per cent possession in front of their own supporters. While Jakirović's side are comfortable defending deep, they are by no means passive out of possession. Although the East Yorkshire side rank comparatively low for overall pressed sequences, they have proved particularly dangerous when winning possession in advanced areas. Only Bournemouth, Everton and Ipswich have recorded more high turnovers leading to shots this season, while Hull's three goals from high turnovers are the most in the Premier League. In this regard, Brentford would be wise to keep an eye on Hull's Algerian right winger Mohamed Belloumi, who already has three Premier League goals to his name this term. Belloumi ranks joint-eighth for successful dribbles, alongside Chelsea's Cole Palmer, while his fierce work rate is reflected by the fact he is also fifth for tackles won. That sort of appetite to compete and win duels will be paramount this weekend, as will quality and decision-making once the ball has been secured. As wild as it sounds now, Hull City were among the bookies’ favourites for relegation in the Championship last season. They faced significant restrictions on transfer spending across the summer of 2025 and winter 2026, while Sergej Jakirović was a new manager without any prior experience in English football. BBC Sport pundits Aaron Paul and Jobi McAnuff tipped them to finish 22nd and Opta’s supercomputer gave them a 16.7 per cent chance of finishing in the drop zone. In the early weeks and months, that didn’t seem like too much of a stretch; they won only two of their first eight league games. But then Jakirović started to get a tune out of his band of brothers. Their best period came between 10 December and 3 February. During a run of 11 games, they won eight, drew two and lost one, climbing as high as third, only four points behind leaders Coventry. But it didn’t last. They won four of the next 15 and a play-off place was only secured after a final-day comeback win at home to Norwich. In the semi-finals, they left it relatively late, but beat Millwall 2-0 in the second leg, and on aggregate, to secure a place in the final. Initially, they thought they were going to be meeting Southampton at Wembley, but the ‘Spygate’ saga and Saints’ subsequent expulsion left them with just four days to prepare to face Middlesbrough following their reinstatement. And just when a typically tepid final looked to be heading to extra-time, Oli McBurnie struck a 95th-minute winner to send the Tigers up for the first time in nine years. It was also the first time since 2010 that the team finishing sixth had gone on to win the play-offs. While going up against all odds was inspiring, Hull were written off again prior to the beginning of this season. In response to the criticism, Jakirović said: “I’ve seen all the predictions, but it’s a great motivation to prove them wrong because we don’t have anything to lose.” Two months into the season and they’ve done that in abundance already. The Tigers stunned Manchester United at MKM Stadium on the opening weekend, held Aston Villa to a goalless draw a fortnight later, and have come from behind to draw 2-2 against both Chelsea and Everton. They are under no illusions about the fact they are likely to be in the relegation picture, but they are building the foundations and picking up the points that will allow them to put up a fight. If they maintain their current points-per-game average of 1.29, they would finish on 49 points - and no team has ever been relegated in a 38-game Premier League season having picked up 43 points. Opta’s supercomputer is currently predicting them to finish 15th. It won’t be as simple as that, though. There will be rough patches - it’s inevitable. But if Hull maintain their spirit - and there’s nothing to suggest they won’t - they will cause some problems. Sergej Jakirović had a long, nomadic playing career as a centre-back, which took him to Croatia, Austria, Slovakia, Slovenia and Bulgaria. He earned five senior caps for Bosnia-Herzegovina and retired in 2017 after a second spell with Croatian lower league side Matija Gubec. He quickly jumped into management with Croatian second-tier side Sesvete, for whom he had played over 60 league games across two separate spells. He guided them to a fourth-place finish in 2017/18, then moved on to the top flight with Gorica. They finished fifth in their first season after promotion, but he was sacked in February 2020. Just under two months later, he joined Maribor in Slovenia, but lasted just 13 games. At the end of 2020, Jakirović took over at Zrinjski Mostar in the city of his birth and in 2021/22 - his only full campaign at the club - he was named Manager of the Season after guiding the club to the Bosnian Premier League title. He left in November 2022 and returned to Croatia, where he spent nine months with Rijeka, another of his former employers as a player. Next came 13 months at Dinamo Zagreb, where he won the title and Croatian Cup double in 2023/24. A crushing 9-2 defeat to Bayern Munich in their first Champions League game of 2024/25 spelled the end of his time in the Croatian capital. He moved on to Kayserispor in Turkey in January 2025, but stayed only until early June, when he signed a two-year deal at Hull. BBC Radio Humberside presenter James Hoggarth provides the lowdown on Hull. "They are very good at shutting down spaces, very good at closing down on the ball and have been solid defensively so far," he told brentfordfc.com. "That back three, particularly John Egan, who Brentford fans will know, has been resolute and very organised. Organisation is the key word. "They have played with a back five effectively all season, with Lewie Coyle and Ryan Giles as overlapping full-backs. "They are snappy in midfield and, if Matt Crooks plays, you can expect a tackle. If Tim Iroegbunam comes in, he will get on the ball and ping passes around to get things going. "Ultimately, it is built on that organisational steel and, in that sense, starts from the back. You can even expect Oli McBurnie to be defending on corners and late on in the game, trying to win things and get under the skin. "This is not a team that will kick you, by any means; it is just a team that is strong and plays for each other." The Merseyside referee has overseen 15 Bees games in his career so far, with the first dating back to 2017 and his most recent match involving the west Londoners being last season's trip to Tottenham Hotspur. Jones has dished out 24 yellow cards in the seven games he has had the whistle for in 2026/27. A Saïd Benrahma hat-trick inspired Brentford to a comfortable victory against Hull in East Yorkshire. Ollie Watkins was also on target, with a Reece Burke own goal completing the scoring for the Bees. Vantage London
