volume 16,  Article number: 33232 (2026) Cite this article A total of 29 patients with severe kyphosis deformity secondary to ankylosing spondylitis underwent posterior spinal osteotomy from October 2017 to April 2023, with intraoperative ST occurring in 7 cases. The primary surgical modification involved the application of V-shaped cobalt-chromium-molybdenum (CoCrMo) alloy rod and changing its place position in the pedicle screws for create displacement between rod and screw, subsequent locking of the screw facilitated a lifting reduction, ensuring accurate alignment and minimizing vertebral displacement. Clinical and radiographic data were collected for all 29 patients. Patient-Reported Outcome were assessed using Oswestry disability index(ODI) and the Scoliosis Research Society-22 (SRS-22) questionnaire for comparative analysis in addition. A total of 29 patients successfully underwent surgery. There were no significant differences in general characteristics between the 7 patients who experienced ST and the 22 patients who did not. Both groups showed significant improvements in sagittal alignment postoperatively, though no significant differences were observed between them. In the ST group, the global kyphosis (GK) improved from 88.3° ± 15.0 to 28.9° ± 20.7, Pelvic tilt(PT) decreased from 34.5°± 20.0 to 18.5° ± 12.8,while in the non-ST group, GK improved from 86.6° ± 28.1 to 30.9° ± 23.0, PT improved from 34.3° ± 15.5 to 26.1° ± 12.5. STs were corrected from 5.4mm ± 1.3 to 1.0mm ± 1.3, with no patients experienced neurological complications postoperatively. ODI improved from 42.6 ± 15.2 to 16.3 ± 7.2 in the ST group, and from 52.5 ± 12.6 to 22.6 ± 11.7 in the non-ST group. SRS-22 scores improved from 10.9±1.7 to 13.8±1.7 in the ST group, and from 10.3±2.6 to 13.9±1.9 in the non-ST group, both improved significantly. The novel surgical technique, utilizing V-shaped CoCrMo rod repositioning within the pedicle screw construct and subsequent lifting reduction, is a safe and effective approach for correcting ST in patients with kyphosis deformity secondary to ankylosing spondylitis. Rigid thoracolumbar kyphosis is a characteristic deformity of ankylosing spondylitis and may lead to severe sagittal imbalance and functional limitation, often requiring corrective osteotomy1,2. Pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO) is widely used to restore sagittal alignment in these patients and has demonstrated satisfactory radiographic and clinical outcomes in multiple series1,2,3. However, sagittal translation (ST) at the osteotomy site remains a notable intraoperative complication of thoracolumbar PSO. ST is defined as unintended anterior or posterior displacement between adjacent vertebrae during osteotomy closure and has been reported in 10.4%–30.4% of patients undergoing PSO for ankylosing spondylitis4,5,6. Lee et al. reported that sagittal translation may result from inadequate control of the osteotomy segment in the rigid, osteoporotic spine typical of ankylosing spondylitis. Posterior translation was found to be associated with delayed union and an increased need for revision surgery4. Park et al. identified a higher modified Stoke Ankylosing Spondylitis Spine Score (mSASSS) as a significant risk factor for sagittal translation following thoracolumbar PSO, and transient neurological symptoms were observed in some patients of 30.2%6. Several technical modifications have been proposed to reduce the risk of ST during thoracolumbar PSO, including the temporary use of connecting rods and the placement of structural support at the osteotomy site, such as inserted cages5,7. Although these measures are effective in prevention, they offer limited guidance for intraoperative correction once sagittal translation has already occurred. However, few studies have addressed how sagittal translation should be managed once it occurs during thoracolumbar osteotomy. As a result, practical intraoperative salvage strategies remain poorly defined, which may compromise neurological safety and surgical outcomes. Accordingly, we describe a technique using pre-contoured V-shaped rods and a lifting maneuver achieved through rod repositioning to facilitate controlled reduction of sagittal translation. Twenty-nine patients who were preoperatively diagnosed with kyphosis deformity secondary to ankylosing spondylitis from October 2017 to April 2023 were enrolled. All patients required osteotomy surgery to correct sagittal imbalance and the inability to maintain a horizontal gaze while standing. In preoperative planning, nine patients were scheduled for single-level osteotomy, while 20 patients were scheduled for two-level osteotomy. All procedures were conducted by a single surgical team and followed up for more than 1 year. A total of 7 vertebral segments in 7 patients experienced ST during the surgeries, all of which were corrected using V-shaped rod repositioning and lifting reduction method intraoperatively. The general data, including age, height, and weight, as well as preoperative osteotomy plans (osteotomy segments and angles), surgery duration, blood loss, intraoperative ST and whether residual ST persisted postoperatively, were documented for each patient. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS version 22.0 for Windows (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation. Paired t-tests were used to compare parameters and clinical outcome measurements before and after osteotomy. Categorical variables were analyzed to assess associations between groups. The Chi-square test was used for comparisons when all expected cell frequencies were ≥5. Fisher’s exact test was applied to ensure accurate probability estimation with small expected frequencies (<5). A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The V-shaped rod used in this procedure was fabricated from a cobalt–chromium–molybdenum (CoCrMo) alloy (Wego Ortho Materials Co., Ltd.). The rod was initially provided as a straight rod measuring 50 cm in length with a diameter of 5.5 mm and was compatible with a standard 5.5mm pedicle screw system. It was not a pre-contoured implant. During surgery, the rod was cut to the appropriate length based on the planned instrumentation levels. According to the preoperative osteotomy plan, the rod was manually pre-bent to match the intended osteotomy angle. The bending angle was subsequently fine-tuned intraoperatively and confirmed using a protractor to ensure consistency with the planned osteotomy correction. For pedicle screw reinforcement, bone cement augmentation was applied to the vertebrae immediately above and below the osteotomy site. Cement was injected along the pedicle screw trajectories to enhance fixation strength. In cases without intraoperative cement leakage and when vertebral body volume permitted, approximately 2.5–3.0 mL of cement was used per screw. All procedures were performed under general anesthesia with continuous intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring. Patients were positioned prone on an adjustable operating frame to provide stable thoracic and abdominal support. A standard posterior midline approach was used, with sequential dissection through the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and fascia, followed by subperiosteal exposure of the targeted vertebrae. Pedicle screws were inserted into the non-osteotomized vertebrae according to the preoperative plan, and fixation stability was confirmed with bone cement augmentation, approximately 2.5–3.0 mL of cement per screw for reinforcement. Posterior column osteotomy was then performed at the planned levels using an ultrasonic bone scalpel and osteotome. The laminae were resected to expose the spinal canal, bilateral nerve roots were carefully decompressed and mobilized, and the lateral walls of the intervertebral spaces were bluntly separated. Bilateral bone resection was carried out to create a V-shaped osteotomy. Osteotomy closure was facilitated by adjusting the operating frame while the assistant elevated the thorax. Temporary fixation was achieved using pre-contoured V-shaped CoCrMo rods. Intraoperative fluoroscopy was used to confirm satisfactory correction consistent with the preoperative plan. After closure, the graft bed was thoroughly irrigated, meticulous hemostasis was achieved, and the resected bone was trimmed and used as local autograft at the osteotomy site. Transverse connectors and negative-pressure drainage were applied, and the wound was closed in layers under sterile conditions. In most cases, ST was characterized by anterior displacement of the proximal osteotomy segment relative to the distal segment in the sagittal plane. After preliminary closure of the osteotomy, fixation was initially limited to one or two pedicle screws above and below the collapsed osteotomized vertebra. Adjustment of torso support was performed by an assistant beneath the operating table. Intraoperative fluoroscopy was used to assess the initial correction. When ST was recognized, one side of the rod–screw construct was maintained in a fixed position, while the screws on the contralateral side were gradually loosened. A rod-holding forceps was used to grasp the rod, which was gently oscillated and translated distally. The extent of distal translation was determined based on the severity of the observed ST. After completion of distal translation of the V-shaped rod, the distal screws were fully tightened. At this stage, a gap was typically observed between the rod and the proximal screw heads, indicating available space for subsequent locking and controlled reduction. Along the axis of the rod, a distractor was gently applied between the screws at both ends of the osteotomy to create a controlled gap at the osteotomy site, facilitating vertebral translation during the reduction maneuver. After stabilizing the rod, the screws were gradually tightened using a T-shaped locking screwdriver. Once fixation on one side was completed, the same sequence of rod translation and reduction was repeated on the contralateral side. After alternating reduction on both sides was completed, controlled compression was applied to close the osteotomy gap. This maneuver achieved definitive ST reduction and final closure of the osteotomy. A schematic illustration of the step-by-step ST reduction technique is shown in Fig. 1. Step 1. Upon recognition of ST, the proximal set screws were loosened to allow distal repositioning of the pre-contoured V-shaped rod. Step 2.Displacement between the screw and the connecting rod was then observed after adjustment. Step 3. With the distal pedicle screws and connecting rod held firmly, gradual locking of the set screws was performed to lift the proximal vertebral segment using “T” locking screwdriver, thereby correcting ST. Step 4. Final reduction of ST was achieved by controlled closure of the osteotomy surface. All radiographic parameters were assessed using standing full-length lateral spine X-rays taken preoperatively and postoperatively for all included patients. General parameters of the sagittal vertical axis and the chin-brow vertical angle were recorded pre- and postoperatively. CT imaging was utilized to evaluate bone quality, detect and assess the severity of Andersson lesions, and plan the placement of pedicle screws. Due to the severity and rigidity of thoracolumbar kyphosis in some patients, not all underwent magnetic resonance imaging. ST refers to the relative anterior or posterior displacement between adjacent vertebrae at the osteotomy site in the sagittal plane. Intraoperative ST was diagnosed based on visible displacement of the posterior vertebral walls during osteotomy closure. No numeric cutoff value was defined; instead, any visible step-off of the posterior vertebral wall was considered clinically significant. ST was assessed through direct intraoperative observation and fluoroscopic imaging. According to the direction of displacement, ST was classified as anterior translation (forward displacement of the proximal vertebral segment relative to the distal segment) or posterior translation (backward displacement of the proximal segment relative to the distal segment). Quantification of ST was performed by measuring the distance between the posterior margins of adjacent vertebrae at the osteotomy site. Intraoperatively, fluoroscopy was used to visualize and calibrate vertebral positioning, with the posterior vertebral wall step-off serving as the primary landmark for displacement assessment. Intraoperative measurements were obtained using fluoroscopy, with intact vertebral endplates of non-osteotomized segments—identified on preoperative standing full-length lateral spine radiographs and measured using the Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS)—serving as reference landmarks to estimate the degree of ST intraoperatively. Postoperative ST was measured on standing full-length lateral spine radiographs using PACS. Global Kyphosis (GK) is defined as the angle between the upper and the lower vertebra that together form the maximum sagittal kyphosis, as measured on a standing full-length lateral spine X-ray. This angle reflects the severity of the sagittal plane kyphotic deformity. The distance from the plumb line passing through the center of C7 to the posterior superior corner of the S1 vertebra.Lumbar Lordosis (LL): The angle formed between the upper endplate of L1 and the upper endplate of S1. Lordosis is considered negative and kyphosis positive. The angle between the line from the midpoint of the bilateral femoral heads to the midpoint of S1 and the vertical line passing through the S1 center. The angle formed between the line from the center of the femoral heads to the center of the S1 upper endplate and a line perpendicular to the S1 upper endplate. The angle between the upper endplate of T4 and the lower endplate of T12. The angle between the upper endplate of T10 and the lower endplate of L2. The angle between the line connecting the chin to the brow and the vertical line of gravity. All complications occurring during the perioperative period were recorded, including but not limited to cerebrospinal fluid leaks, dural tears, neurological symptoms, abdominal pain, and wound infections. Patient-Reported Outcome Measures were measured through ODI, and quality of life was evaluted by using SRS-22 score. A total of 29 patients with kyphosis deformity secondary to ankylosing spondylitis underwent osteotomy correction. Intraoperative sagittal translation (ST) occurred in 7 patients (1 single-level and 6 double-level osteotomies; mean age 46.1 ± 5.6 years, range 37–54 years), while the remaining 22 patients had no ST (8 single-level and 14 double-level osteotomies; mean age 46.1 ± 10.1 years, range 29–64 years). The demographic and intraoperative characteristics of patients with ST are summarized in Table 1, and a comparative analysis of patients with and without ST is shown in Table 2. No significant differences were observed between the two groups in baseline features, planned osteotomy angles, or perioperative complications. Radiographic analysis demonstrated that osteotomy significantly improved sagittal alignment across the entire cohort. The global kyphosis (GK) angle, sagittal vertical axis (SVA), lumbar lordosis (LL), and chin–brow vertical angle (CBVA) all showed marked improvement postoperatively (Table 3). However, when comparing patients with and without intraoperative ST, no significant differences in alignment parameters were detected at any time point. Patient-reported outcomes confirmed the functional benefits of surgery. Both the ODI and SRS-22 scores improved significantly from baseline to final follow-up (Table 4), indicating enhanced function and quality of life. Again, no statistically significant differences were found between patients with and without ST. A 54-year-old male(Case 6) was diagnosed with kyphotic deformity due to ankylosing spondylitis, with a 39-year history of the condition. He was scheduled for a single-level PSO at the L2 vertebral level, with a planned osteotomy angle of 30 degrees to correct the kyphotic deformity. During the procedure, ST occurred after the initial closure (Figure 2a), and there was a sudden change in intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring signals. After intraoperative adjustment of the pre-bent V-shaped rod (Figure 3) by altering the bending point and reopening the osteotomy, ST was improved(Figure 2b). Although a residual ST of approximately 3 mm was observed on the postoperative X-ray, intraoperative adjustments led to an improvement in neurophysiological signals. Postoperative follow-up showed improvements in sagittal balance, as confirmed by lateral radiographs (Figure 4a, b). Intraoperative fluoroscopic images demonstrating sagittal translation (ST) and its correction. (a) Intraoperative lateral fluoroscopic image showing anterior sagittal translation at the osteotomy site immediately after initial closure above 7 mm; (b) Final intraoperative fluoroscopic image confirming correction of ST. Preoperative and postoperative radiographic outcomes of the representative case. (a, b) Preoperative and postoperative standing lateral full-spine radiograph demonstrating satisfactory correction of kyphosis. In ankylosing spondylitis, chronic inflammation leads to progressive ossification and fusion of the vertebral segments, resulting in a rigid spine and progressive kyphotic deformity8,9. PSO, originally developed to correct such deformities, has been shown to be an effective surgical technique10,11. In our series, all patients demonstrated radiographic and clinical improvement following posterior column osteotomy, including correction of global kyphosis and restoration of pelvic alignment. ST remains a recognized complication during PSO for kyphotic deformity secondary to ankylosing spondylitis. In addition to its potential neurological consequences, intraoperative ST may increase technical difficulty and disrupt surgical workflow, which can indirectly affect patient confidence. Severe ST may result in posterior column displacement, spinal cord compression, or transient changes in intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, often increasing intraoperative stress for the surgical team. Although previous reports have suggested that spinal canal remodeling occurs to varying degrees over time, even in patients with ST, this process does not necessarily lead to long-term neurological deterioration12. Persistent vertebral displacement remains a source of uncertainty for both surgeons and patients. In the study by Park et al., four patients developed residual neurological complications following surgery among a total of 16 cases complicated by intraoperative sagittal translation, with a mean translation of 7.2 mm (range, 3.5–11.7 mm)6. In this study, we show that a technique combining pre-contoured V-shaped rod repositioning with a lifting reduction maneuver provides an effective intraoperative approach for correcting sagittal translation and mitigating its clinical impact. Repositioning of the V-shaped rod creates controlled displacement between the pedicle screws and the connecting rod, allowing realignment through distraction of the previously closed osteotomy surface. Within this minimally distracted osteotomy environment, cement-augmented pedicle screws at both the proximal and distal segments provide sufficient pullout strength to support controlled reduction, ensuring that the locking of the screw cap does not result in loosening due to inadequate pull-out strength, thereby preventing internal fixation failure13. Locking of the screw promotes axial translation of the proximal vertebral segments toward the connecting rod, thereby reducing vertebra–rod displacement and, in turn, ST. However, this technique may increase technical complexity during the procedure. Nevertheless, in our experience, it has been effective in reducing the magnitude of sagittal translation. Even when residual ST persisted after correction, its magnitude was generally reduced to an acceptable level and did not compromise radiographic outcomes or patient-reported function. No significant differences were observed between patients who experienced intraoperative sagittal translation and those who did not. Current literature provides limited evidence on the intraoperative correction of ST, as previous studies have primarily focused on preventive approaches. Arun et al. described the use of temporary connecting rods to stabilize the osteotomy site during closure, thereby reducing the risk of uncontrolled vertebral displacement7. Hu et al. reported that cage insertion at the osteotomy site could decrease the incidence of ST by providing anterior column support, although this approach may increase procedural complexity and invasiveness5. Zhang et al. introduced an adjustable prone positioning frame that enables gradual and controlled closure during deformity correction, aiming to minimize sudden collapse and translation through optimized intraoperative positioning14. Most previously reported strategies have focused on preventing ST rather than managing it once it occurs intraoperatively. However, ST may still occur despite careful planning and preventive measures, particularly in patients with severe kyphosis, or poor bone quality6. The technique proposed in the present study differs conceptually from these preventive approaches. By repositioning a pre-contoured V-shaped rod and utilizing a lifting reduction mechanism through controlled rod–screw displacement, this method allows active correction of ST after its occurrence. Importantly, this approach does not require additional anterior support, secondary surgical corridors, or specialized equipment, and can be integrated into standard posterior instrumentation workflows. Therefore, rather than serving as an alternative preventive strategy, the present technique may be considered a salvage and corrective option for intraoperative sagittal translation during osteotomy, complementing existing preventive methods and expanding the surgical options for managing this challenging complication. The occurrence of ST decreases as surgeons gain experience, with a corresponding decline in its incidence over time. Similar to ST reduction, the key principle in reducing this type of displacement is to deliberately create relative displacement between the pedicle screws of the slipped vertebra or displaced osteotomy segment and the connecting rod, and then achieve reduction by gradually eliminating this displacement. In previous procedures for mild spondylolisthesis, we have commonly adopted a strategy of adjusting screw insertion depth to intentionally modulate the degree of rod–screw engagement. However, in cases with more pronounced slippage, screw depth cannot be adjusted without limitation, as excessive adjustment may compromise screw purchase and increase the risk of loosening. Yi introduced a reduction technique for lumbar spondylolisthesis using a self-designed T-shaped tool15. During surgery, manual force was applied to control the direction of the instrument, allowing elevation of the slipped vertebra, and reduction was achieved through sequential tightening of the pedicle screws. Xu et al. described a percutaneous rod-traction technique in which the distal screws were first secured, followed by traction of the rod into the proximal screw heads and subsequent screw locking, thereby achieving reduction of lumbar spondylolisthesis16. Similarly, Zhang et al. reported the reduction process for retrolisthesis, in which the intervertebral space was appropriately distracted while the slipped vertebra was elevated and reduced17. This reduction strategy, which relies on adjusting the connecting rod rather than altering screw insertion depth, has proven to be effective in clinical practice, and we fully agree with this viewpoint. The technique described in this study allows controlled intraoperative correction of sagittal translation using principles similar to standard pedicle screw-rod reduction techniques. Despite its relative technical simplicity, it may reduce intraoperative stress and the risk of neurological complications. One limitation of this study is the relatively small sample size, which may have influenced the findings. In addition, we did not quantitatively analyze the extent of rod adjustment required to correct ST. Although a theoretical geometric relationship exists, it was difficult to quantitatively define the relationship between ST and rod displacement based on the pre-contoured angle of the V-shaped rod. In theory, the distance of rod translation required to correct ST can be calculated using the formula: (ST distance)/sin α, where α represents the pre-contoured angle of the V-shaped rod, which also corresponds to the planned osteotomy angle. This relationship warrants further validation in future studies. The use of a pre-contoured V-shaped rod, designed according to the preoperative angle, along with the adjustment of the bending point to create relative displacement and the locking of the screw to lift the vertebrae which causes ST, effectively addresses and corrects ST during surgery. This method offers a practical and reliable solution for managing ST in clinical practice. The data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. Wen, Y. G. et al. title: We Drive Ferrari’s New V-12 Supercar with a Manual Transmission, but There’s a Twist - Car and Driver
content: Ferrari’s 12Cilindri Manuale brings back the gated manual transmission in a very 2026 way. Ferraris have always been defined by their engines, but never in so literal a fashion as the 12Cilindri. As you probably guessed, cilindri is Italian for “cylinders.” If you don’t want to pidgin it, the name is Dodici Cilindri. Literal as it may be, though, 12Cilindri describes two Ferraris: the brand’s flagship grand tourer and its vaguely SUV-ish four-door. The name is less ambiguous than if Toyota were to dub a vehicle the 4Cylinder, but still not exactly definitive. Enter the 12Cilindri Manuale. Now you know we’re talking about the two-seat Ferrari, because that’s the only Ferrari available with a manuale transmission. But the manual is a bit of smoke and mirrors. Rather, it’s solenoids and Hall-effect sensors, the 21st-century equivalent of smoke and mirrors. Mechanically, the Manuale’s eight-speed dual-clutch is the same transaxle you’ll find between the standard 12Cilindri’s rear wheels. But here, a third pedal gives the driver electronic control of those clutches, and a dainty aluminum shifter juking through a machined aluminum plate lets the driver select among the first six ratios. The car’s computers do the work of rods and levers, communicating the motion of those components to the clutches and shift forks in the transaxle. See all results for new 2027 Ferrari 12Cilindri for sale near 50317 One look at the shifter tells you it is not meant to be manhandled. (Decades ago, one of our editors managed to snap the lever clean off the gated shifter in a V-12 supercar from some other Italian automaker; he sells insurance now.) Both the clutch pedal and the shifter are light in their action, less tactile than we’d hoped. It’s hard to discern through your foot where the friction point is but easier to pay attention to when the car starts moving. Given the 12Cilindri’s light-switch throttle, be extremely judicious lest you overrev that big 6.5-liter, make noob noises, and/or smoke a clutch creeping away from a stop. But be careful you don’t stall it, which is a real possibility. Drive it poorly, and the 12Cilindri Manuale allows the driver to make all manner of stick-shift blunders in the interest of rewarding deeper engagement. Let the clutch out too quickly while underway, and you’re punished with jerky engagement. Downshift without blipping the throttle and you’ll be thrown against the seatbelt—there’s no automatic rev matching here. Grab the wrong gear, and you’re in the wrong gear. The exception is if your shift would zing the engine beyond its 9500-rpm redline. Do that, and the stick will hang up halfway into the gate, like a normal manual waiting for the synchros to engage but without that horrible grinding noise. The 12Cilindri Manuale will punish the driver, but it will not punish itself. Walking us through the shifter’s operation, an engineer winces at this phrasing. “Perhaps ‘punish’ is a harsh word,” he corrects us. “It gives you lessons.” In other words, unless you endanger the machine, the Manuale acts exactly as if it has a normal manual transmission. Clutch-dump burnout? Sure. Grab second gear to keep the Michelin Pilot Sport S5s spinning past 70 mph? You bet. See all results for new 2027 Ferrari 12Cilindri for sale near 50317 Judged against other cars with a gated shifter between the seats flicking forks in a gearbox on the rear axle, though, nothing about the Manuale suggests artificiality. And while you don’t get the sense that you’re feeling gear teeth engage through the lever, the metallic snick-snick that accompanies each shift is precisely what we’d hoped for. The shifter gates appear to be more tightly spaced than they are; you don’t need to worry about grabbing fifth when aiming for third. Move too conservatively upshifting from second, however, and you will end up beached on the aluminum isthmus delineating first from third. The Manuale’s light clutch pedal and low-effort shifter are consistent with the 12Cilindri’s other controls. Feathery steering and brakes are central to the car’s light and playful demeanor, belying its 186.3-inch length and estimated 3900 pounds (some 10 inches longer and 400 pounds heavier than the commoner’s front-engine sports car, the C7 Chevrolet Corvette). The 12Cilindri floats through turns and dances in response to driver inputs. Get on it, and the delicate clutch and shifter action fit in perfectly with the other controls. If your clutch leg starts to cramp, you encounter traffic, or you’re cruising on the highway and want seventh and eighth gear, push the “D” button on the center console and the Manuale will revert to automatic operation. When you’re ready to reengage, just step on the clutch, slide the shifter into an appropriate gear, and the fun begins again. Ferrari will only build 1499 copies of the 12Cilindri Manuale, an homage to the cubic-centimeter displacement of the V-12 in the very first Ferrari. We’re guessing the brand decided to build roughly 1500 and then someone connected that figure rather than the initial production target being “however many cc’s the 125 S’s V-12 was.” Luckily for Ferrari, there are lots of numbers in its past, so it can hang a historical reference on just about any integer. A number Ferrari didn’t explain is the more than $200,000 upcharge for the Manuale variant. Speaking of numbers, the Manuale is not as quick as the regular 12Cilindri. Ferrari chief test driver Raffaele De Simone says he can just about match the standard car’s acceleration times while working the clutch and shifter. Of course, he’s been involved in the development of every Prancing Horse for more than 20 years. You will be slower. But you will not care. A couple of tenths are a price well worth paying for the lost joy of working a gated manual shifter. 2027 Ferrari 12Cilindri ManualeVehicle Type: front-engine, rear-wheel-drive, 2-passenger, 2-door hatchback ENGINEDOHC 48-valve V-12, aluminum block and heads, direct fuel injectionDisplacement: 396 in3, 6496 cm3Power: 819 hp @ 9250 rpmTorque: 500 lb-ft @ 7250 rpm DIMENSIONSWheelbase: 106.3 inLength: 186.3 inWidth: 79.0 inHeight: 50.9 inCargo Volume: 10 ft3Curb Weight (C/D est): 3900 lb PERFORMANCE (C/D EST)60 mph: 2.7 sec100 mph: 5.7 sec1/4-Mile: 10.4 secTop Speed: 211 mph EPA FUEL ECONOMY (C/D EST)Combined/City/Highway: 14/12/19 mpg Jared Gall started his career with Car and Driver as an unpaid intern, but has now worked here more than half of his life. title: Roy V. Staley - Gladwin County Record & Beaverton Clarion
content:
Roy V. Staley, 84, of Coleman, joyously ran into the arms of his Lord and Savior Jesus Christ on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026 following a sudden cardiac arrest at his home. Roy was born July 12, 1942 in Midland, the son of the late Bernard and Marita (Huss) Staley. He was raised on the family farm with his two sisters, Barb and Pam, and brother, Bob, and attended Coleman schools. Roy married the love of his life, Linda K. Vannest, on Jan. 28, 1967 in Gladwin. They were married for 59 years and were completely devoted to each other and to their family. They were virtually inseparable, particularly following Roy’s retirement. Together, Roy and Linda raised their children, Troy and Lorinda, with endless love and a deep faith in the Lord. To them, God and family were everything, and it was evident in the way they lived their lives and raised their family. Roy had an incredibly strong work ethic throughout his life. As a young boy, he milked cows at his family farm. At the age of 16, Roy started working at Robinson Industries. He graduated from Central Michigan University in 1964, earned a Master’s degree in 1967, and began his career as a business teacher in 1968. He retired from the Meridian Public Schools in 1997 after 29 years of service. While teaching, he also raised pigs and grew strawberries. As he neared retirement, he began growing tomatoes and other produce and did so for the past 29 years, generously giving the proceeds to his granddaughters for their college education funds. Roy loved the Lord with all his heart, and he and Linda taught their children to love the Lord as well. He faithfully attended the Beaverton Church of the Nazarene, along with Linda, and their children and granddaughters. Everyone who knows Roy and Linda know that the greatest joy of their lives is their three granddaughters: Gracie, Olivia, and Rachel. To their granddaughters, they were “Bop and Grandma”. To Bop and Grandma, their granddaughters were “the girls” and they were their whole world. They were completely and totally devoted to them, never missing a ball game, track meet, cross country meet, school event, or church program. They took absolute delight in everything they did and gave them one of the very best gifts grandparents can give: time. And even more importantly, they gave them a legacy of faith in Jesus. Roy and Linda enjoyed attending church together with their whole family, camping at Grand Marais and Manistique, fishing, hunting, taking family trips to Dollywood, visiting friends at the Old Brick Bakery and Coffeehouse in Coleman, and attending Sunday School at their dear friend Mary Geeck’s home. Roy is survived by his beloved and devoted wife, Linda of Coleman; his son and best friend, Troy and Shelly Staley of Coleman; his much loved daughter, Lorinda and Tom Dubay of Coleman; and his precious and beloved granddaughters: Grace Staley, Olivia Dubay, and Rachel Dubay. He is also survived by his brother, Robert and Marcy Staley of Coleman; sisters: Barbara Zietz and Pamela and Donald White of Gladwin; brothers-in-law: Byron Vannest of Gladwin, and Mike and Karen Steinkraus of Gladwin; sisters-in-law: LaNeel Vannest of Midland, Karen Vannest of Appleton, WI; and Susan Vannest of Gladwin; several nieces and nephews. In addition to his parents, Roy was preceded in death by brothers-inlaw, Timothy Zietz, Wayne Vannest, Harold Vannest, Dennis Vannest, and Mark Vannest, and sister-in-law, Janet Vannest. Funeral services were held at 11 a.m. on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026 at the Beaverton Church of the Nazarene, with Rev. Martin Hodge officiating. Burial took place in the Warren Township Cemetery, Coleman. Friends attended the visitation at O’Laughlin Funeral Home, Inc. on Sunday from 2-6 p.m. and at the church on Monday starting at 10 a.m. until the time of service. Memorials are suggested to the Beaverton Church of the Nazarene. Gladwin County Record and Beaverton Clarion

title: Tree Week: Jamie V. Robertson: In Search of Osman’s Ghost - Lenscratch
content: ©Jamie V. Robertson, Osman in the Swamp Archival Inkjet Print 18 x 24 inches 2024 I met Jamie V. Robertson at the FotoFest reviews in Houston, and was immediately struck by the quiet strength of her images of southern swamplands. The pictures are taken with Infrared film, which makes the tree foliage seem luminescent. This haunting effect is tied into her exploration of the maroon colonies of runaway slaves that lived deep in the swamp. The farther in the escapees went, the less likely it was that the slave catchers would follow you. Robertson skillfully adds historical drawings of runaways to her images to help the viewer visualize the terror those people felt. ©Jamie V. Robertson,Spirited Away Archival Inkjet Print 18 x 24 inches 2024 In Search of Osman’s Ghost is a photographic series that explores the connection between humanity and nature by illuminating maroonage in the Southern Swamplands. Informed by the literary works of Toni Morrison, bell hooks, Lucille Clifton, and Édouard Glissant, the Southern Swamp is reframed as a living collaborator for runaway slaves in colonial America. Its ‘rememory’ of maroons, self-liberated formerly enslaved people who lived on the fringes of colonial America, is explored through black and white infrared photography and archival illustrations. Infrared film, which has applications in science, medicine, and paranormal studies, captures images outside of the visible light spectrum, giving a surreal and otherworldly experience of the environment. Can a swamp dream? What or who does it dream of? Does it remember its brief alliance with those seeking freedom? The surrealist nature of infrared images allows for the exploration of memory in the landscape. The Great Dismal Swamp in Virginia, the Everglades in Florida, and the Bas Du Fleuve of New Orleans were sites of maroonage where Africans and African Americans made their dream of freedom a reality. This series looks at the Swamp, the maroons, and how their alliance defied colonial standards of living. In Search of Osman’s Ghost invites the viewer to explore this counternarrative of America’s history to consider their own relationship to the natural world. ©Jamie V. Robertson, A Place To Steal Oneself Away II Inkjet Print 72 x 46 inches 2025 Jamie V. Robertson (B. 1988 American) is a visual artist and educator working in photography and video. Born and raised in Houston, her Texas roots inform her practice as she examines the environment of the American South and its relationship to Black counter-narratives. Through research, writing, photography, and video art, her work excavates a history of Black defiance, contending with the vilified and monolithic narrative of the Southern United States. Deeply influenced by the works of Toni Morrison, bell hooks, and Lucile Clifton, her creative practice embraces a Black Feminist Hauntology, a framework that acknowledges the spectral presence in Southern land through untold histories. Her approach to image-making fluidly oscillates between analog and digital processes, with an emphasis on black and white infrared film. Robertson utilizes text, archival images, and found imagery as materials and companions to her work to oppose the hierarchy of high and low culture. Jamie earned an MFA in Studio Art from the University of Houston and an MS in Art Therapy from Florida State University. Robertson is an Assistant Professor at Old Dominion University and works between Texas and Virginia. Currently, her research explores the Great Dismal Swamp and maroonage. ©Jamie V. Robertson, The Runaway Archival Inkjet Print 18 x 24 inches 2024 Can you tell me what drew you to photograph this project, and how you felt when you were doing it. I have always had an interest in the natural world and its intersection with Black History. My early work dealt with my family’s history and relationship to the Texas Freedom Colony, Egypt Community, outside of Centerville, TX. My family has held land there since emancipation. The term “Freedom Colony” comes from the work of Dr. Andrea Roberts at UVA. In hindsight the move into marronage in North America feels like a natural shift. There is a lot of overlap between maroon colonies and freedom colonies. I have always known about maroons in other parts of the Americas like Jamaica, Brazil and Colombia but I had never heard them mentioned in the United States. It was a podcast episode with historian Marcus Nevis, on his book, City of Refuge, that really piqued my interest. As I began to do more research I became excited by this history of rebellion and resistance. ©Jamie V. Robertson, A Place To Steal Oneself Away III Inkjet Print 72 x 46 inches 2025 Who was Osman, and was he a real person who was related to you? This series is a move away from my family history work and the beginnings of looking at collective histories. Osman was a real person who lived in the Great Dismal Swamp. The only details we have of him come from David Hunter Strother in 1856 who was traveling through the swamp after a visit to an enslaved workers’ camp. He sees Osman briefly in the thicket of the swamp armed with a rifle. And just like a figment of the imagination, he was gone. Osman was a maroon but colonial society would have probably referred to him as a fugitive or runaway. Maroons were people who ran away from slavery and built autonomous communities in the hinterlands. In Jamaica, they lived in the mountains, in the U.S. , the Swamp was the primary location. These communities were difficult for colonial authorities to reach on purpose. Outside New Orleans, which I am hoping to photograph in the near future, St. Jean Malo, a maroon leader, had signs posted with warnings informing trespassers they were entering maroon territory. ©Jamie V. Robertson, Kudzu and Clouds Archival Inkjet Print 18 x 24 inches 2025 How did you first find out about the maroon people and the slaves who escaped to freedom in the swamps? I’m not really sure when I first learned of maroons. I knew Black enclaves of resistance existed throughout the Americas. However, these were things I learned outside of the academic environment. The nuance of the lives of Black people during slavery is always missing from K-12 education. For instance, the lives of enslaved people in cities like Norfolk and New Orleans were very different from those who were enslaved on the plantations in the Sea Islands. Enslaved people in cities worked in various trades and often moved about the city unsupervised versus those who worked in the fields were under constant surveillance by an overseer.That specificity is worth noting. Maroonage is a byproduct of the system of slavery and essential to understanding that time period as well as the fact that Black people resisted slavery. ©Jamie V. Robertson, An Obscure Place To Hide 18 x 24 inches Archival Inkjet Print 2024 It must have been very difficult living conditions, with constant fear of being captured. Do you know what happened to them? The swamp absolutely has its dangers. In the Life of Moses Grandy, he talks about escaping to the Great Dismal Swamp. One night while sleeping he felt the wet nose of some animal sniffing him. Moses eventually escaped North and was more or less passing through the swamp. Historians called this Petit Marronage because people’s stay was short term. As for the people who really lived there, we really don’t know what they thought of the environment other than it was a fantastic place to hide because all these dangers protected them from slave catchers who really didn’t want to venture deep into that terrain. One historian, Ryne Beddard, suggests that some of the first Africans who escaped into the swamp more than likely saw it as a sacred place because of their own cultural cosmologies. I like this reading the best because we tend to think about history from our position in the present and this reading honors what would have been the interior culture of enslaved people. As for what happened to maroons, it varies. In Jamaica , they still live in the mountains until this day. As for the United States, I would imagine that some mixed in with various indigenous people and maybe others came out of the swamp after emancipation. ©Jamie V. Robertson, Beware the Hounds 18 x 24 inches Archival Inkjet Print 2026 How do your images allude to the people and natural environment? My series, In Search of Osman’s Ghost, uses black and white infrared photographs of southern swamplands and archival illustrations of maroons, runaways and resistance leaders to make visible the historic alliance between Black Americans and the natural world. Infrared film, which has applications in science, medicine, and paranormal studies, captures images outside of the visible light spectrum, giving a surreal and otherworldly experience of the environment. My process is two-fold. I spend time photographing historic wetland environments with black and white infrared film. As of late, I have started looking at expired rolls of films like Efke IR 820 and Macophot because they go deeper into the electromagnetic spectrum than the newer stocks. The images can range from soft to sharp depending on the brand and film size.The second part involves researching digital archives for images of maroons, runaways and fugitives. Maroons materialize in these images through the use of Photoshop. Conceptually, I have begun to think about these images as surreal. D. Scot Miller’s 2009 manifesto titled, ‘Call it Afro-Surreal’ really resonated with me. He states,“Afro-Surreal presupposes that beyond this visible world, there is an invisible world striving to manifest, and it is our job to uncover it. Like the African Surrealists, Afro-Surrealists recognize that nature (including human nature) generates more surreal experiences than any other process could hope to produce.”These sentiments along with the writings of Toni Morrison and bell hooks inform my framework of living memory in the landscape. ©Jamie V. Robertson, An Obscure Place To Hide II 18 x 24 inches Archival Inkjet Print 2026 I’d like to know what it was like to work in the swamp? Did you have issues with your equipment? Did you photograph from a boat or from the shore? I really enjoy being out in the swamp. I photograph primarily in Virginia, Texas and Louisiana. I’m hoping to hit more Southern states in the coming years. In spite of the general term, ‘swamp’, they all feel different. The Great Dismal Swamp is very still and there are parts that don’t feel much like a traditional swamp at all. In Texas, I primarily focus on the bayous. In Houston alone the bayous range from heavily polluted ( like the one I grew up by) to wild. I often make my photographs from the shoreline or the side of the road. Sometimes, I lower my POV to imply being on the water. But also wetlands are low-lying areas. Some of the best things are happening pretty low to the ground. I haven’t had many issues with equipment other than an shutter release breaking or wishing that I had brought more film. As for wildlife, I have yet to see a snake, alligator or bear (knock on wood) but there are lots of insects, turtles and aquatic mammals like otters.The mosquitos can be brutal so I always carry insect repellent. I don’t feel afraid being out there even when I am alone because a lot of my experience is mediated by being on trails or walking over a cypress swamp via a boardwalk. It’s not hard to use your imagination about how the place would look without so much human intervention. ©Jamie V. Robertson, A Maroon’s Dream 18 x 24 inches Archival Inkjet Print 2026 ©Jamie V. Robertson, John Horse (Juan Caballo) 18 x 24 inches Archival Inkjet Print 2025 ©Jamie V. Robertson, The Great Dismal Swamp 24 x 36 inches Archival Pigment Print 2025 ©Jamie V. title: Como v Man Utd preview: Key stats and player info - Yahoo Sports
content: After the hostile surroundings of Atletico Madrid and Leeds United, Manchester United's third successive away game takes them to the rather more picturesque lakeside setting of Como. The atmosphere may be less intimidating, but the task will be no easier against a side whose rapid rise under Cesc Fabregas has taken them into Europe for the first time. Promoted to Serie A just two years ago, the Biancoblu pipped AC Milan and Juventus to Champions League qualification last season and marked their debut with a stirring 4-1 win over RB Leipzig. They were brought back to earth by last week's 3-2 defeat at Feyenoord, but Fabregas insisted any blame for that result lay with him, not his squad. He says he told them: "Don't hang your heads. These are nights that help you grow." Another formative test awaits against the three-time European champions, although the Red Devils head to Italy short on confidence. Head coach Michael Carrick likened Sunday's draw at Leeds to a "fresh start", saying he was "encouraged by a lot of things" he saw at Elland Road, but the result extended United's winless run to six matches. They have not gone seven games without a victory since 2015. Italian sides have won just two of their past 16 games against Manchester United (D4, L10). Como are the second side in Champions League history who didn't pick one domestic player in their starting XI for their first two matches. The other was Moldova's Sheriff Tiraspol in 2021. The Argentine number 10 is Como's crown jewel and chief creative influence. He contributed 12 goals and six assists in 35 Serie A appearances last season and was named the league's best midfielder. The son of former Argentina international Pablo Paz, who ended his career in Spain, Nico was born in Tenerife and progressed through Real Madrid's academy before joining Como in 2024. Fabregas spent the final year of his glittering playing career in Serie B with Como before briefly coaching their under-19s. He took charge of the first team as caretaker in November 2023, then assisted Welshman Osian Roberts while completing his coaching qualifications. After they led Como to promotion, Roberts moved into a development role and Fabregas became permanent head coach. Como's multi-national squad features players from 13 different countries, including England's Trevoh Chalobah. Chalobah has quickly earned a starting role, though he was forced off injured at the weekend. His former Chelsea team-mate Robert Sanchez, who is on loan from the Blues, has mainly served as understudy to French goalkeeper Jean Butez, playing twice so far.

title: Trump v. United States — That says it all - Bleeding Heartland
content:

Herb Strentz was dean of the Drake School of Journalism from 1975 to 1988 and professor there until retirement in 2004. He was executive secretary of the Iowa Freedom of Information Council from its founding in 1976 to 2000. Try as one might, I defy you to find a better concise description of what’s at stake in the upcoming election than Trump v. United States—the U.S. Supreme Court ruling decided by a 6-3 majority on July 1, 2024. Think about it: The President vs. the United States of America. Our short-term future might be in 3-D: Daily Doses of Disaster, or Democracy’s Doses of Despair. So what’s wrong with Trump v. United States? In a word, everything. However, my focus today is on the hypocrisy inherent in claiming to be both bipartisan and pro-Trump. The Supreme Court’s conservative majority — shaped by Iowa’s U.S. Senator Chuck Grassley — has given President Donald Trump the equivalent of a Monopoly get-out-of-jail-free card. We are saddled with “a landmark decision…holding that presidential immunity from criminal prosecution presumptively extends to all of a president’s “official acts” – with absolute immunity for official acts within an exclusive presidential authority that Congress cannot regulate.” Trump has the Monopoly card, and we get a wannabe king not being held accountable by Congress or the courts. Maybe on November 3, voters will finally hold Trump accountable for his continuous disasters, aided by Iowa’s four U.S. Representatives — the honorable Zach Nunn, the honorable Ashley Hinson, the honorable Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and the honorable Randy Feenstra — and our two U.S. senators — the honorable Grassley and the honorable Joni Ernst. Mocking the six as “honorable” ties in well with the hypocrisy of so much campaign rhetoric these days, as the Iowa delegation abandons the constitutional balance of power our founding fathers envisioned. And it ties in well with the despair many feel about the coming election. Whatever its outcome, we face two more years of Trump, and the lingering fears about what threats lie ahead after his reign ends. (One is that the vulgar plans for a money-making Trump presidential library will also bring rot to the presidential library system — as though today’s decay of democracy is not enough to fret about.) Forget about corn and soybeans. Iowa’s Congressional delegation is more than knee deep in a harvest of hypocrisy. When announcing her candidacy for Ernst’s Senate seat in September 2025, Hinson pledged to be Trump’s “strongest ally” in the chamber, vowing “Mr. President…I will not let you down.” That vow — conspicuous by its absence in the Hinson campaign today — likely will be the order of the day if Iowans elect Hinson to the Senate. That is what an analysis by the international news agency Reuters suggests: Two-thirds of Republican candidates running for the House and Senate have broken with President Donald Trump on key policy matters or sought to minimize their associations with him. An analysis by Reuters, which examined voting records, campaign materials, and public statements across 62 high-stakes races ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, identified 41 candidates attempting to create space between themselves and the administration as the president’s low popularity threatens the party’s congressional majorities. […] The strategy appears designed to appeal to independent voters while avoiding a complete break with the leader of their party. For her part, Hinson still plays some Trump cards, like the fomenting fear of immigrants. A Hinson campaign ad attacks her Democratic opponent, State Senator Josh Turek, for pointing out that immigrants do have legal rights, even though they are not citizens. Reports from KCRG-TV of Cedar Rapids and the national fact-checker Politifact have faulted Hinson’s attacks. Meanwhile, another Trump supporter seeking re-election, the “honorable” Nunn, has resorted to playground taunts in his campaign against State Senator Sarah Trone Garriott. Despite Trone Garriott’s lengthy and impressive record of public service, Nunn ridicules her as “kooky”— a taunt masquerading as a guide to reasoned decision making. Nunn’s use of the “kooky” label is contemptible. When fresh out of college, Trone Garriott was a VISTA (Voluteers in Service to America) worker in New Mexico as an advocate for victims of domestic abuse. She then worked in similar capacity while attending Harvard Divinity School and comforting families and children as a hospital chaplain. She served as a Lutheran minister and worked for the Des Moines Area Religious Council in serving the needy and building bridges among the different faiths in Central Iowa. “Kooky,” “kooky,” “kooky” is how Nunn characterizes that background, throwing in some misleading statements about her legislative work. (Disclosure: I became a friend of Sarah’s when she was an associate pastor at Faith Lutheran Church in Clive.) Nunn and Hinson both ignore the fact that Trone Garriott and Turek crossed party lines in the legislature to vote with Republicans on some issues. More than ten years ago, Iowans heard a warning about the woes in store for us if Grassley became chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee. But the warning was botched and — as it has turned out — the woes were greatly underestimated. The context: in 2014, Democrat Bruce Braley and Republican Joni Ernst vied to see who would succeed Democratic Senator Tom Harkin. At a fundraiser in Texas, Braley warned trial lawyers of what would happen if Republicans gained control of the Senate and Grassley —”a farmer from Iowa who never went to law school, never practiced law” — were in charge of the Judiciary Committee. Concern about Grassley’s lack of a legal background was merited. But Republicans turned Braley’s perceived slur against farmers into a major campaign issue, putting “a farmer from Iowa” in countless ads that boosted Ernst’s campaign. Republicans did flip the Senate in 2014, and Grassley became committee chairman. Bleeding Heartland contributor Rick Morain provided one of the most glaring examples of Grassley’s partisanship in a post on April 23, 2025. It’s well worth reading. The adjective “glaring” is warranted, given how often Grassley claims to be “bipartisan.” But his role in shaping the judiciary for Trump belies that assessment. Nine years later, Grassley acknowledged that in 2016 he either misled or lied about reasons for blocking President Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nomination of the well-qualified Merrick Garland. That paved the way for Trump’s controversial appointment of Neil Gorsuch to the court, and was an early sign of the demise of our “checks and balances” system of government. It will be far from a satisfactory answer. But at least on November 3, it would be a start. Voters can support the United States in a retake on Trump v. United States. Shame on all who voted for him over the years (especially Dems) and to all who have really failed to report to the public on how extreme a figure he (and his team like Mike Davis) has been these many years. Good thing the new director of the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa is on the case….

title: Legendary UH submersible Pisces V begins new chapter at Bishop Museum - University of Hawaii System
content:
After nearly four decades of uncovering historic mysteries of the Pacific Ocean, the deep-sea submersible Pisces V is embarking on a new journey on land. The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa donated the legendary three-person research vessel to the Bernice Pauahi Bishop Museum, ensuring that its legacy of deep-ocean exploration, volcanic research and historic maritime discoveries will be preserved for generations to come. “The donation ensures the submersible’s storied past will be celebrated and shared with museum visitors from Hawaiʻi and around the world,” said Chip Fletcher, dean of the UH Mānoa School of Ocean and Earth Science and Technology (SOEST), home of the Hawaiʻi Undersea Research Laboratory (HURL). HURL operated Pisces V along with its sister submersible, Pisces IV, for decades. However, after years in storage with no prospect of federal funding for refurbishment or redeployment, UH made the decision to entrust the historic craft to the museum. In 1985, UH acquired Pisces V, anchoring HURL’s growing undersea capabilities. Its unique maneuverability, size and depth range, operating at depths up to 6,500 feet, made it the ideal platform for navigating complex terrain and gracefully exploring delicate ecosystems. “Operating as the only United States (U.S.) deep submergence facility based in the Pacific Rim, HURL’s work with Pisces V revolutionized oceanography across several fronts,” said Terry Kerby, veteran Pisces V pilot and HURL operations director. “The submersibles were fine-tuned to adapt to the demands of operating effectively in the wide range of terrain and conditions of undersea volcanoes, seamounts in Papahānaumokuākea and beyond, maritime heritage site surveys, salvage operations of lost instruments and vehicles, and decades of pipeline support for the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaiʻi Authority cold water pipe systems. It is exciting to see the Pisces V and this legacy preserved at the Bishop Museum.” Close to home, Pisces V, enabled unprecedented exploration of the seamounts and coral reefs of the Main and Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. The submersible made more dives on Hawaiʻi’s active underwater volcano, Kamaʻehuakanaloa (previously known as Lōʻihi Seamount), than any other submersible. HURL submersibles also pioneered research on mesophotic and deep-sea coral reefs off Maui and throughout the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, conducting vital impact assessments on commercial fishing damage. Throughout the Pacific basin, the submersible ferried teams of researchers on voyages of discovery to places no human had seen before. In 2005, Pisces V embarked on a five-month expedition across the Pacific, exploring active submarine volcanoes along the Kermadec Arc near New Zealand. “Each of these dives were unique, each different,” Kerby shared. “We discovered multiple new species and by combining submersible operations with human divers, we explored deep-sea coral ecosystems in a new way.” A MAYJAH Night: Homecoming Concert & Makers’ Market Have a story idea or a question?Contact news@hawaii.edu If required, information contained on this website can be made available in an alternative format upon request.

title: Thomson Reuters v. ROSS: Third Circuit Recognizes a Licensing Market for AI Training Data (via Passle) - Baker Botts
content: On September 29, 2026, the Third Circuit issued what appears to be the first federal appellate decision on whether training AI on copyrighted material is fair use. In Thomson Reuters v. ROSS Intelligence, the court affirmed that case-law headnotes are copyrightable and that using them to train a non-generative legal-research tool was not fair use. Early coverage has emphasized footnote 7, which distinguishes AI that "cannot generate original expression" from generative models, and the court's finding that "the evidence shows that the market for licensing headnotes as text to train AI is rapidly developing." Less attention has gone to how courts will test evidence of that market. Under the fourth factor, the court found harm to the original market and to the value of the headnotes, and it also recognized a potential derivative market for licensing them as training data. It cited evidence that the copyright owner was using its headnotes "as training data for its own AI search products" and held that the absence of licenses to third parties "does not disprove that a market exists to do so." Consistent with Warhol, the burden remained on the party asserting fair use. This reasoning is difficult to square with two June 2025 decisions from the Northern District of California. Judge Alsup assumed that a market for licensing books as training data could develop but held that it "is not one the Copyright Act entitles Authors to exploit." Judge Chhabria held that whether such a market "exists or is likely to develop is irrelevant," because counting lost licensing fees for a transformative use as market harm would make the fourth factor circular. The Third Circuit did not address circularity, although it had already concluded that the use was "minimally transformative, at best." Read together, the decisions may suggest that the first factor operates as a threshold. If a court finds the training use transformative, licensing evidence may be legally irrelevant under the California approach; if it does not, that evidence may decide the fourth factor. Where courts do weigh licensing evidence, the analysis may resemble a reasonable royalty dispute in a patent case. Courts may have to decide whether a proffered license is comparable to the use at issue, whether a bundled deal reflects a price for training at all, and how much weight to give a license negotiated to settle litigation. The Federal Circuit has held that licenses used to set a royalty must be "commensurate with what the defendant has appropriated" and has cautioned that "litigation itself can skew the results of the hypothetical negotiation" (ResQNet). In EcoFactor, the court held under Rule 702 that a damages expert should not have been allowed to testify that prior licenses reflected a per-unit royalty the licenses themselves did not support. The Supreme Court used similar reasoning in Google v. Oracle, giving little weight under the fourth factor to licensing negotiations that "concerned much more than 37 packages of declaring code." AI fair use cases may see the same comparability disputes and Rule 702 challenges to licensing experts. The analogy has limits: the burden of proof runs the other way, and patent law has no equivalent to the circularity concern. For companies on either side of a training-data deal, the practical takeaway is that license terms may become evidence in fair use litigation. Companies should watch whether further review takes up the circularity question, whether the next district court follows the Third Circuit, and whether courts begin testing these licenses the way patent courts test comparable licenses.

This past weekend, Michie Stadium celebrated an Army victory over Florida Atlantic University, accepted two reunion gift presentations, and welcomed the newest member of the Army Mule Team. Together, these milestones reflected the ongoing momentum for the progress of West Point’s programs, facilities, and cadets. In celebration of its 20th reunion, the West Point Class of 2006 presented a $725,000 reunion gift supporting both Goethals Hall and the West Point Press. The gift, presented by Class President Brandon Archuleta and classmate Sam Russo, establishes a new record for the largest 20th-reunion gift in Academy history. The Class of 2016 also marked a reunion milestone with a $300,000 gift in celebration of its 10th reunion. Presented by Class President EJ Coleman and Class Vice President Jake Tyer, the gift to Goethals Hall and the Modern War Institute marks the class’s first reunion gift to West Point. Both class gifts advance the Academy’s academic and military missions and create continued opportunities for cadets to learn, lead, and prepare for future service. Scheduled to welcome its first classes in January 2027, Goethals Hall will house the Departments of Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering, Civil & Environmental Engineering, Electrical Engineering & Computer Science, and Systems Engineering. The state-of-the-art facility honors Major General George Washington Goethals, Class of 1880, the Army engineer who supervised the construction and opening of the Panama Canal. The Modern War Institute connects academic study with the challenges of contemporary conflict. Recently, it hosted the Class of 2006 Modern War Conference, centered on “Deterrence in the Pacific.” Military, defense, and national security experts joined cadets for five panels exploring strategic competition in the Indo-Pacific, deterrence, future warfare, and the U.S. Army’s role in the region. These transformational gifts to the Margin of Excellence provide resources and opportunities that enrich the cadet experience beyond what federal funding alone can provide. The weekend also included an on-field recognition of Steve Townes ’75, who presented Ranger V, the newest member of the Army Mule Team. The Army mules are a cherished West Point icon, embodying the traditions and spirit of the Academy. Ranger V is only the third female mule to join the program. Her distinctive dunskin coloring adds a new look to the team, giving the Army Mule Team its own version of black and gold. Since 2001, Steve and Suzy Townes have endowed the Army Mule Program, providing resources to sustain the team in perpetuity. Their generosity helps preserve the mule as a living symbol of the West Point brand, embodying the strength, resilience, and steadfastness associated with the Academy while maintaining its familiar presence at Army athletic events and Academy celebrations. These moments reflect the Long Gray Line’s commitment to leadership that extends well beyond the uniform. Through the generosity of alumni, friends of the Academy, and dedicated benefactors, West Point’s mission and traditions remain strong, providing future generations of cadets with opportunities to develop into the leaders of character our nation requires. 698 Mills Road

title: Cadillac F1 Driver Checo Perez Gets a Limited Edition Escalade V Named After Him - The Drive
content:
Published				

					Oct 20, 2026 1:23 PM EDT The Daily Brief wraps up the biggest stories and our exclusive reporting on the auto industry and car culture. The Formula 1 circus is descending on Texas as I type this, then heading to Mexico next week for one of the calendar’s most cherished races. With Sergio Perez back on the grid this year, Cadillac (the automaker and the F1 team) is throwing a big party on both sides of the border to celebrate not just the Mexican racer, but also its second race ever on American soil. It’s just revealed an awesome cowboy-inspired livery, as well as a “Checo Perez Edition” Escalade V. This special-edition, three-row SUV doesn’t get any performance upgrades, but that’s probably fine, since its 6.2-liter, supercharged V8 already produces 682 horsepower, enough to hit 60 mph in just 4.4 seconds. It does get some neat visual enhancements that may be enough to persuade the biggest F1 fans to spring for one of the only 11 units that will be produced. Why 11? That’s Perez’s racing number. Some of these enhancements include blacked-out badging (that’s supposedly a different tone from the other black badges already available), monochromatic Escalade badging on the front and rear of the SUV, an exposed carbon fiber engine cover, aluminum pedals, unique graphics in the ground projections, a numbered plaque, and an exclusive welcome kit. They’ll be offered in only two colors closely linked to the Cadillac F1 car: black or white. The only kicker: All 11 units are allotted to the Mexican market, so if any die-hard fans in the U.S. are willing to spend the equivalent of $222,500 for one, they’ll have to head south. title: About Gellert Global Group Corp. v. Trump - Liberty Justice Center
content: The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration’s use of Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose tariffs and import restrictions on Canadian goods on behalf of Gellert Global Group, a third-generation family-run food business that imports and distributes food products across the U.S. Gellert also works with American farmers and producers to bring U.S. food products to international markets. The lawsuit seeks relief for Gellert and a proposed class of American importers affected by the tariffs. On October 20, 2026, the Liberty Justice Center filed a lawsuit in the U.S. Court of International Trade challenging the administration’s Section 338 action. Alongside the complaint, the Liberty Justice Center filed a motion seeking a preliminary injunction to block collection of the tariffs and summary judgment in Gellert’s favor. The lawsuit argues that Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 superseded or limits the use of Section 338, and that even if Section 338 still applies, the administration has failed to establish the statutory basis for its sweeping tariffs. The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote. The Section 338 tariffs impose a 50% tax on the Canadian cheeses Gellert Global Group imports, while Canadian retaliation also affects the American cheeses its Canadian division sells in Canada. Those costs do not stop with one company. One of Gellert’s Canadian cheese suppliers purchases milk from dairy farmers in upstate New York, processes it into brie in Canada and ships the finished cheese back to American customers. The tariffs therefore disrupt a supply chain that supports American farmers, businesses and consumers. The stakes extend far beyond one business and far beyond Canada. If Section 338 can be used this way against Canada today, it can be used against any country tomorrow. That would give future presidents of either party sweeping power to impose tariffs and import restrictions without meaningful congressional control. The case builds on the Liberty Justice Center’s successful Supreme Court challenge to tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), its successful challenge to Section 122 tariffs in the Court of International Trade, now on appeal, and its pending Section 301 litigation. Each case seeks to enforce the constitutional and statutory limits on presidential tariff authority. The Liberty Justice Center asks the court to declare the Section 338 tariffs unlawful, stop their collection, and order refunds, with applicable interest, for affected importers. Jeffrey M. Schwab serves as Senior Counsel and Director of Litigation at the Liberty Justice Center, where he litigates cases to protect the rights to free speech, economic liberty, private property and other Constitutional rights in both federal and state courts across the country. Reilly Stephens is a Senior Counsel at Liberty Justice Center, where he assists in cases to protect the rights to free speech, economic liberty, private property, and other Constitutional rights in courts across the country. For generations, Gellert Global Group has helped bring food from around the world to American tables. The family-run business, headquartered in Elizabeth, New Jersey, connects farmers, food producers and suppliers around the globe with American grocery stores, restaurants, hotels and manufacturers. Its business depends on longstanding relationships—and the ability to move products reliably across international borders. Now, the administration’s decision to impose steep tariffs and outright bans on certain Canadian imports threatens those relationships, increases costs and disrupts the supply chains that American businesses and consumers depend on. “Our customers are personal friends. Our employees are personal friends. People we buy from are personal friends.” — George G. Gellert, Chairman of the Board, Gellert Global Group Gellert Global Group traces its roots to 1945, when Leon Rubin and Herbert Moeller founded Atalanta Corporation as an importer of Polish food products. What began as one family business has grown into a network of food-importing and distribution companies serving customers across the United States. Today, the group sources more than 4,000 unique food items from more than 60 countries, supplying retailers, distributors, foodservice chains, hotels, cruise lines and food manufacturers. Its products include specialty cheeses, fruits and vegetables, nuts, seafood and other ingredients used throughout the American food industry. Many consumers encounter Gellert’s products without ever knowing the family business that helped bring them to market. Behind those products are American workers, farmers, truckers, warehouse operators, retailers and restaurant owners who depend on the international supply chains that companies like Gellert have spent generations building. The Gellert family remains closely involved in the business, with family members serving in leadership roles across the organization, including Co-Chief Executive Officer Thomas Gellert and Co-Chief Executive Officer Andrew Gellert. The family has built its business around a principle passed down through generations: suppliers are partners, not simply vendors, and lasting relationships are essential to providing quality products to American customers. Gellert Global Group works with suppliers across more than 1,000 approved manufacturing sites worldwide to bring a diverse range of food products to market. Its food safety and quality assurance team oversees standards across that global supply base. But Gellert’s global business is not simply about bringing foreign products into America. It also helps American producers reach customers across our borders. And nowhere is that relationship more apparent than in its trade with Canada. Consider what happens to milk produced by dairy farmers in upstate New York. One of Gellert’s businesses exports that American milk to Canada, where it is made into specialty cheese. The finished cheese then crosses the border again, returning to the United States to help meet demand for products that American producers do not supply in sufficient quantities. The American farmer has a customer. The Canadian cheese producer has a supplier. American distributors, restaurants, retailers and consumers receive a product they want. And an American family business helps make the entire process possible. What might appear on paper to be a simple import from Canada is actually the final step in a supply chain that began on an American farm. Disrupting that trade can hurt American businesses on both sides of the border. How Tariffs and Import Bans Threaten Gellert’s Business The administration has invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose additional tariffs of 50 percent on certain Canadian products and prohibit the importation of others altogether. These measures threaten American businesses like Gellert that depend on cross-border trade. For Gellert, these are not abstract trade disputes. They threaten relationships built over generations, disrupt business decisions made months or years in advance, and create uncertainty for the American companies and workers that depend on its products. Why Gellert Global Group Is Challenging the Administration’s Use of Section 338 Represented by the Liberty Justice Center, Gellert Global Group is challenging the administration’s use of Section 338 because the Constitution gives Congress—not the president—the power to impose tariffs and regulate foreign commerce. The lawsuit argues that Section 338—a provision of the Tariff Act of 1930 directed at foreign discrimination against U.S. commerce—is not an all-purpose tool for imposing sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises. The case is not about whether tariffs are good or bad trade policy. It is about who has the constitutional authority to impose them—and whether the president can invoke a nearly century-old statute to impose tariffs and import bans beyond the limits Congress established. For three generations, Gellert Global Group has built a business connecting American farmers, food producers and consumers with markets around the world. Its lawsuit seeks to protect those relationships and uphold a fundamental constitutional principle: The president must operate within the limits of the authority Congress has given him.
